courses.title: Ch 8 · Introduction to Trigonometry
courses.summary: The six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle in a right triangle, finding all ratios from one, exact values at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, and proving identities using sin²A + cos²A = 1 and its two partners.
outcomes: Learners can define sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec and cot for an acute angle
Learners can find all ratios given one ratio
Learners can derive and use values at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°
Learners can prove the three Pythagorean identities and use them in proofs
Learners can evaluate trigonometric expressions accurately

lessons.title: Trigonometric ratios of an acute angle

scenes.text: A school is building a ramp: it must rise 1 m over a 12 m slope.
The angle the ramp makes with the ground decides how hard it is to push a wheelchair.
Ratios of sides in the right triangle — rise/slope, run/slope — describe that angle. These are trigonometric ratios.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
In ΔABC right-angled at B, for the acute angle A: side **opposite** A is BC, side **adjacent** to A is AB, **hypotenuse** AC.

- sin A = opposite/hypotenuse = BC/AC
- cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse = AB/AC
- tan A = opposite/adjacent = BC/AB
- cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A

Also **tan A = sin A / cos A** and cot A = cos A / sin A. The ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle (similar triangles!).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — AB = 24 cm, BC = 7 cm, right angle at B
steps.body:
**Step 1:** AC = √(24² + 7²) = √(576 + 49) = √625 = 25 cm.

**Step 2:** sin A = 7/25, cos A = 24/25, tan A = 7/24.

**Step 3:** For angle C, opposite side is AB: sin C = 24/25, cos C = 7/25.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — PQR right-angled at Q, PR + QR = 25 cm, PQ = 5 cm
steps.body:
Let QR = x, PR = 25 − x. Then (25 − x)² = x² + 25 → 625 − 50x = 25 → x = 12. So QR = 12, PR = 13.

sin P = QR/PR = 12/13, cos P = 5/13, tan P = 12/5.

steps.title: Memory aid
steps.body: Say 'Some People Have Curly Black Hair Through Proper Brushing': sin = P/H, cos = B/H, tan = P/B (P = perpendicular/opposite, B = base/adjacent, H = hypotenuse).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing sin as an abbreviation of a number: 'sin × A' is meaningless; sin A is one number.
- Using the wrong 'opposite' side when the angle changes from A to C.
- Thinking sin A can be more than 1 — the hypotenuse is the longest side, so 0 < sin A < 1 for acute A.

activity.prompt: ΔABC is right-angled at B with AB = 4, BC = 3, AC = 5. Match each ratio of angle A with its value.

quiz.q: In ΔABC right-angled at B, tan A =
quiz.why: tan A = opposite/adjacent. With the right angle at B, the side opposite A is BC and the adjacent side is AB, so tan A = BC/AB.

quiz.q: cosec A is the reciprocal of
quiz.why: cosec A = 1/sin A, so it is the reciprocal of sin A. Sec A is the reciprocal of cos A.

quiz.q: For an acute angle, the value of cos A always lies
quiz.why: For an acute angle, adjacent < hypotenuse, so cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse is between 0 and 1.

quiz.q: If AB = 24 and BC = 7 with right angle at B, sin A =
quiz.why: AC = √(24² + 7²) = 25. sin A = opposite/hypotenuse = BC/AC = 7/25.

quiz.q: tan A equals
quiz.why: tan A = (opposite/hyp) ÷ (adjacent/hyp) = sin A/cos A.

scenes.text: A puzzle card says: 'sin A = 3/4'. Find the other five ratios.
Raghav draws a right triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 4.
Pythagoras gives the third side √7 — and then every ratio follows.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Draw a right triangle and label two sides from the given ratio (use k as a scale: 3k and 4k).
2. Find the third side with Pythagoras.
3. Write every ratio from the triangle.

Or use identities: cos A = √(1 − sin²A) for acute A.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — sin A = 3/4
steps.body:
Opposite = 3k, hypotenuse = 4k, adjacent = √(16k² − 9k²) = √7 k.

cos A = √7/4, tan A = 3/√7, cosec A = 4/3, sec A = 4/√7, cot A = √7/3.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — 15 cot A = 8
steps.body:
cot A = 8/15 → adjacent 8k, opposite 15k, hypotenuse 17k.

**sin A = 15/17, sec A = 17/8.**

steps.title: Solved example 3 — evaluate an expression
steps.body:
If cot θ = 7/8, evaluate (1 + sin θ)(1 − sin θ)/[(1 + cos θ)(1 − cos θ)].

This is (1 − sin²θ)/(1 − cos²θ) = cos²θ/sin²θ = cot²θ = **49/64**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — 3 tan A = 4, check an identity
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the scale k (sides are 3k and 4k, not necessarily 3 and 4) — the ratios are the same either way.
- Mixing up which side is opposite.
- Leaving √ in denominators is acceptable, but simplify where asked (3/√7 = 3√7/7).

activity.prompt: If cos A = 12/13 (A acute), find tan A as a decimal to 3 places (it equals 5/12).

quiz.q: If tan A = 4/3, sin A =
quiz.why: tan A = 4/3 means opposite 4, adjacent 3, so hypotenuse 5. sin A = 4/5.

quiz.q: If sin A = 1/2, cos A =
If sec θ = 13/12, sin θ =
quiz.why: sec θ = 13/12 means hypotenuse 13 and adjacent 12, so the opposite side is √(169 − 144) = 5. sin θ = 5/13.

quiz.q: If cot θ = 7/8, then cot²θ =
If 15 cot A = 8, then sec A =
quiz.why: cot A = 8/15 means adjacent 8, opposite 15, so hypotenuse 17. sec A = 17/8.

scenes.text: Every geometry box has two set-squares: 45°–45°–90° and 30°–60°–90°.
Their side ratios are fixed, so their trigonometric values are exact and memorable.
These values appear in almost every board paper.

steps.title: Where the values come from
steps.body:
**45°:** in an isosceles right triangle with legs a, hypotenuse a√2 → sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2, tan 45° = 1.

**30° and 60°:** split an equilateral triangle of side 2a by an altitude: half-base a, altitude a√3 → sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3.

**0° and 90°:** sin 0° = 0, cos 0° = 1, tan 0° = 0; sin 90° = 1, cos 90° = 0, tan 90° not defined.

steps.title: Table
steps.body:
- sin: 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1 (for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)
- cos: 1, √3/2, 1/√2, 1/2, 0
- tan: 0, 1/√3, 1, √3, not defined

Trick: sin values are √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2; cos runs the same list backwards.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — find sides
steps.body: In ΔABC right-angled at B, AC = 6 cm and ∠C = 30°. AB = AC sin 30° = 3 cm, BC = AC cos 30° = 3√3 cm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B (false: sin 60° ≠ sin 30° + sin 30°).
- Claiming tan 90° = ∞ in an answer — say 'not defined'.
- Swapping sin 30° and cos 30°.

activity.prompt: Complete from memory.

quiz.q: sin 60° =
quiz.why: From the 30°–60°–90° triangle with hypotenuse 2, the side opposite 60° is √3, so sin 60° = √3/2.

quiz.q: tan 30° =
quiz.why: In the 30°–60°–90° triangle, tan 30° = 1/√3 (opposite 1, adjacent √3).

quiz.q: (2 tan 30°)/(1 + tan²30°) equals
cos 0° × sin 90° =
quiz.why: cos 0° = 1 and sin 90° = 1, so the product is 1.

quiz.q: If sin(A − B) = 1/2 and cos(A + B) = 1/2, A and B are
quiz.why: sin(A − B) = 1/2 gives A − B = 30°, and cos(A + B) = 1/2 gives A + B = 60°. Adding gives A = 45° and B = 15°.

quiz.q: Which is not defined?
quiz.why: tan 90° = sin 90°/cos 90° = 1/0, which is undefined. The others are defined.

scenes.text: Mehak notices that sin²θ + cos²θ always equals 1, whatever θ she tries.
Dividing that rule by cos²θ or sin²θ creates two more identities.
With these three, long-looking proofs collapse in a few lines.

steps.title: The three identities (0° ≤ A ≤ 90°, where defined)
steps.body:
From AB² + BC² = AC², divide by AC², AB² and BC²:

- **sin²A + cos²A = 1**
- **1 + tan²A = sec²A** (A ≠ 90°)
- **1 + cot²A = cosec²A** (A ≠ 0°)

Useful rearrangements: sec²A − tan²A = 1 = (sec A − tan A)(sec A + tan A); cosec²A − cot²A = 1.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — prove (1 + tan²A)/(1 + cot²A) = tan²A
steps.body: LHS = sec²A / cosec²A = (1/cos²A) ÷ (1/sin²A) = sin²A/cos²A = tan²A = RHS ∎

steps.title: Solved example 2 — prove (sec A + tan A)(1 − sin A) = cos A
steps.body: LHS = [(1 + sin A)/cos A](1 − sin A) = (1 − sin²A)/cos A = cos²A/cos A = cos A = RHS ∎

steps.title: Solved example 3 — prove (cosec θ − cot θ)² = (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ)
steps.body: LHS = [(1 − cos θ)/sin θ]² = (1 − cos θ)²/(1 − cos²θ) = (1 − cos θ)²/[(1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ)] = (1 − cos θ)/(1 + cos θ) ∎

steps.title: Solved example 4 — express in sin
steps.body: Express tan A in terms of sin A: tan A = sin A/cos A = sin A/√(1 − sin²A).

steps.title: Proof strategy
steps.body: Start from the more complicated side. Convert everything to sin and cos. Look for (1 − sin²) or (1 − cos²) patterns. Never 'move terms across' the equals sign in a proof — transform one side until it becomes the other.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing sin²A as sin A² (it means (sin A)²).
- Cancelling terms across a sum: (1 + sin A)/sin A ≠ 1.
- Starting from what you must prove as if it were given.

statements.s: sin²A + cos²A = 1 for every acute angle A.
sec²A + tan²A = 1.
cosec²A − cot²A = 1.
sin A + cos A = 1 for all A.
9 sec²A − 9 tan²A = 9.

quiz.why: 9 sec²A − 9 tan²A = 9(sec²A − tan²A) = 9 × 1 = 9.

quiz.q: (1 + tan θ + sec θ)(1 + cot θ − cosec θ) simplifies to
quiz.why: Expand using sin and cos: [(cos + sin + 1)(sin + cos − 1)]/(sin cos) = [(sin + cos)² − 1]/(sin cos) = 2.

quiz.q: (sec A + tan A)(1 − sin A) =
quiz.why: (sec A + tan A)(1 − sin A) = [(1 + sin A)/cos A](1 − sin A) = (1 − sin²A)/cos A = cos²A/cos A = cos A.

quiz.q: 1 + cot²θ equals
quiz.why: The identity 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ comes from dividing sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 by sin²θ.

quiz.q: If sec θ + tan θ = p, then sec θ − tan θ =
quiz.why: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = sec²θ − tan²θ = 1. So sec θ − tan θ = 1/p.

quiz.q: cos A expressed via cot A is
quiz.why: sin A = 1/√(1 + cot²A) because 1 + cot²A = cosec²A. Then cos A = cot A × sin A = cot A/√(1 + cot²A).

questions.q: sin 30° + cos 60° =
questions.why: sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 60° = 1/2, so the sum is 1.

questions.q: tan 45° =
questions.why: tan 45° = 1, because in an isosceles right triangle opposite and adjacent sides are equal.

questions.q: sec A is the reciprocal of
questions.why: sec A = 1/cos A, so it is the reciprocal of cos A.

questions.q: If sin A = 4/5 (A acute), cos A =
questions.why: sin A = 4/5 means opposite 4, hypotenuse 5, so adjacent is 3 (3–4–5 triangle). cos A = 3/5.

questions.q: sin²60° + cos²60° =
questions.why: sin²A + cos²A = 1 for every angle, so sin²60° + cos²60° = 1. Check: 3/4 + 1/4 = 1.

questions.q: If tan A = √3, then A =
questions.why: tan 60° = √3, so A = 60°. Tan 30° is 1/√3 and tan 45° is 1.

questions.q: Assertion: sin A can be 4/3 for some acute angle A. Reason: the hypotenuse is the longest side of a right triangle.
questions.why: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse and the hypotenuse is the longest side, so sin A < 1. Hence 4/3 is impossible: A is false and R is true.

questions.q: If cos A = 1/2 and A is acute, then sin A + tan A =
If sin θ − cos θ = 0 (θ acute), then sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ =
questions.why: sin θ = cos θ gives θ = 45°. Then sin⁴θ + cos⁴θ = (1/√2)⁴ + (1/√2)⁴ = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

questions.q: Case: A ladder leans against a wall, its foot 2.5 m from the wall and top 6 m high. The ladder length and cos of the angle with the ground are
questions.why: Ladder length = √(2.5² + 6²) = √(6.25 + 36) = √42.25 = 6.5 m. The angle with the ground has cos = 2.5/6.5 = 5/13.

questions.q: For any acute angle A, sec²A − tan²A + sin 30° =
questions.why: sec²A − tan²A = 1 and sin 30° = 1/2, so the sum is 1 + 1/2 = 3/2.

questions.q: If 3 cot A = 4, then (1 − tan²A)/(1 + tan²A) =
If sin A + sin²A = 1, then cos²A + cos⁴A =
questions.why: sin A + sin²A = 1 gives sin A = 1 − sin²A = cos²A. So cos²A + cos⁴A = sin A + sin²A = 1.

questions.q: If tan θ + cot θ = 2 (θ acute), tan²θ + cot²θ =
questions.why: tan θ + cot θ = 2 with tan θ × cot θ = 1 gives tan θ = 1. Squaring: tan²θ + cot²θ + 2 = 4, so tan²θ + cot²θ = 2.

questions.q: The value of (sin A − 2 sin³A)/(2 cos³A − cos A) is
questions.why: The numerator is sin A(1 − 2sin²A) and the denominator is cos A(2cos²A − 1). Since 1 − 2sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = cos²A − sin²A, the expression is sin A/cos A = tan A.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Some Applications of Trigonometry
courses.summary: Heights and distances: line of sight, angles of elevation and depression, and one- and two-triangle problems with towers, kites, ladders, ships and moving observers — every solution set out in board style.
outcomes: Learners can draw a correct figure from a heights-and-distances statement
Learners can identify angles of elevation and depression
Learners can solve single right-triangle problems with tan, sin and cos
Learners can solve two-triangle problems with a common side
Learners can use √3 ≈ 1.732 and √2 ≈ 1.414 to give decimal answers

lessons.title: Line of sight, elevation and depression

scenes.text: Kiran stands in a field looking up at the flag on top of a temple.
The straight line from her eye to the flag is the line of sight; the angle it makes with the horizontal is the angle of elevation.
From the temple top, the priest looks down at Kiran: that angle is the angle of depression.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **Line of sight:** the line from the observer's eye to the object.
- **Angle of elevation:** angle between the line of sight and the horizontal when the object is **above** eye level.
- **Angle of depression:** angle between the line of sight and the horizontal when the object is **below** eye level.

Because the two horizontals are parallel, the **angle of depression from A to B = angle of elevation from B to A** (alternate angles).

steps.title: Which ratio to use
steps.body:
Mark the known side and the side you want relative to the angle:

- opposite & adjacent → **tan**
- opposite & hypotenuse → **sin**
- adjacent & hypotenuse → **cos**

Towers, poles and buildings are vertical; the ground is horizontal — so there is always a right angle.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — read the figure
steps.body: A kite is flying at the end of a 60 m string inclined at 60° to the ground. The string is the hypotenuse, the height is opposite → sin 60° = h/60 → **h = 30√3 ≈ 51.96 m**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — depression to elevation
steps.body: From a 10 m high balcony, the angle of depression of a car is 30°. Then the angle of elevation of the balcony from the car is also 30°. tan 30° = 10/d → **d = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring the angle of depression from the vertical wall instead of the horizontal.
- Forgetting the observer's height when the question gives it (add it to the computed height).
- Using sin when the hypotenuse is not involved.

activity.prompt: Which ratio would you use first?

items.text: Know distance from foot, want height of tower
Know string length of kite, want height
Know ladder length, want distance of its foot from wall
Know height of lighthouse, want distance of ship
Know slide length, want its height

quiz.q: The angle of elevation is measured from
quiz.why: The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal line through the observer's eye to the line of sight.

quiz.q: Angle of depression from A to B equals
options: angle of elevation from B to A
quiz.why: The angle of depression from A to B equals the angle of elevation from B to A, as they are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.

quiz.q: Kite string 60 m at 60°: height is
quiz.why: Height = string × sin 60° = 60 × √3/2 = 30√3 m.

quiz.q: When the opposite and adjacent sides are involved we use
quiz.why: When the opposite and adjacent sides are involved, tan = opposite/adjacent is the right ratio to use.

quiz.q: If the sun's elevation increases, a pole's shadow
quiz.why: Shadow length = h cot θ. As θ increases, cot θ decreases, so the shadow gets shorter.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Some Applications of Trigonometry)

lessons.title: One-triangle problems

scenes.text: An electrician must fix a fault 1.3 m below the top of a 5 m pole.
Her ladder should make 60° with the ground.
Height needed = 3.7 m; sin 60° = 3.7/L gives the ladder length.

steps.title: Board-style layout
steps.body:
1. Draw the figure; name points (A, B, C …).
2. Write 'In right ΔABC, ∠B = 90°'.
3. Write the ratio: tan θ = AB/BC.
4. Substitute and solve; rationalise; give a decimal if asked.
5. Write the final answer with units.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — tower
steps.body: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 30 m from its foot is 30°. h = 30 tan 30° = 30/√3 = **10√3 ≈ 17.32 m**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — broken tree
steps.body: A tree breaks and its top touches the ground 8 m from the foot, making 30° with the ground. Standing part = 8 tan 30° = 8/√3; broken part = 8/cos 30° = 16/√3. Height = 24/√3 = **8√3 ≈ 13.86 m**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — with observer height
steps.body: A 1.5 m tall boy stands 28.5 m from a chimney and sees its top at 45°. Height above his eye = 28.5 tan 45° = 28.5 m. **Chimney = 28.5 + 1.5 = 30 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to add the observer's eye height.
- Rationalising incorrectly: 30/√3 = 10√3, not 30√3.
- Rounding √3 to 1.7 when the question says 1.732.

activity.prompt: A 15 m ladder reaches a window when it makes 60° with the ground. How high is the window? (√3 = 1.732; answer to 2 decimals)

quiz.q: Tower height from 30 m away at 30° elevation:
quiz.why: Height = distance × tan 30° = 30 × 1/√3 = 10√3 m.

quiz.q: Broken tree example: total height
quiz.why: In the broken-tree right triangle the unbroken part and the fallen part give a total height of 8√3 m once the ratios are applied.

quiz.q: A slide of height 1.5 m inclined at 30° has length
quiz.why: sin 30° = height/length, so 1/2 = 1.5/L and L = 3 m.

quiz.q: Shadow of a 6 m pole when the sun's elevation is 60°:
quiz.why: Shadow = height × cot 60° = 6 × 1/√3 = 6/√3 = 2√3 m.

quiz.q: Chimney example height
quiz.why: The right triangle gives the height above eye level, and the observer's eye height of 1.5 m is added. The chimney is 30 m.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Some Applications of Trigonometry)

lessons.title: Two-triangle problems

scenes.text: Sameer sees the top of a tower at 30°. He walks 20 m closer and now sees it at 60°.
He does not know either distance, but there are two right triangles sharing the same height.
Two equations, two unknowns — just like Chapter 3.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body: Let the common side (usually the height h) and an unknown distance x be variables. Write one tan equation from each triangle, then eliminate. Expect answers like 10√3 or 20(√3 − 1).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — walking 20 m
steps.body:
From the near point: h = x tan 60° = x√3. From the far point: h = (x + 20) tan 30° = (x + 20)/√3.

x√3 = (x + 20)/√3 → 3x = x + 20 → x = 10. **h = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m**, and the near point is 10 m from the tower.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — tower on a building
steps.body:
From a point on the ground, the elevations of the bottom and top of a transmission tower on a 20 m building are 45° and 60°.

Distance d = 20 cot 45° = 20 m. Top height = 20 tan 60° = 20√3. **Tower = 20√3 − 20 = 20(√3 − 1) ≈ 14.64 m**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — statue on a pedestal
steps.body: A 1.6 m statue stands on a pedestal. From a point on the ground, the top of the statue is at 60° and the top of the pedestal at 45°. Let pedestal = p, distance = d: d = p (45°) and p + 1.6 = d√3 = p√3 → p(√3 − 1) = 1.6 → **p = 0.8(√3 + 1) ≈ 2.19 m**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — two poles across a road
steps.body: Two equal poles stand on either side of an 80 m road. From a point between them, elevations are 60° and 30°. h = x√3 = (80 − x)/√3 → 3x = 80 − x → x = 20. **h = 20√3 ≈ 34.64 m**; distances 20 m and 60 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the same symbol for two different distances.
- Forgetting that the 'walk' distance is the difference of the two ground distances.
- Rationalising (√3 − 1) denominators wrongly: 1.6/(√3 − 1) = 1.6(√3 + 1)/2.

activity.prompt: Order the solution of 'tower seen at 30° then 60° after walking 20 m closer'.
items: Draw the tower and both observation points
Write h = x√3 for the nearer point
Write h = (x + 20)/√3 for the farther point

quiz.q: In example 1, the tower height is
quiz.why: In example 1 the height comes from tan of the elevation angle times the distance, giving 10√3 m.

quiz.q: Transmission tower height in example 2:
quiz.why: The transmission tower's height is the top height minus the building height, which gives 20(√3 − 1) m.

quiz.q: Pedestal height in example 3 (approx.)
quiz.why: Pedestal height = 0.8 × 2.732 ≈ 2.19 m.

quiz.q: Two-triangle problems usually share
quiz.why: In two-triangle problems the same height usually appears in both triangles. This common side links the two equations.

quiz.q: Poles across an 80 m road with elevations 60° and 30°: each pole is
quiz.why: Let the first pole be x from the point: h = x tan 60° = (80 − x) tan 30°, so √3x = (80 − x)/√3, giving 3x = 80 − x and x = 20. Then h = 20√3 m.

lessons.title: Angles of depression: ships, cars and buildings

scenes.text: From the top of a 75 m lighthouse, a keeper sees two ships, one behind the other, at angles of depression 45° and 30°.
How far apart are the ships?
Convert depression to elevation at each ship and use tan twice.

steps.title: Turning depression into elevation
steps.body: Draw the horizontal at the observer's eye. The angle of depression to an object equals the angle of elevation from the object (alternate angles). Then work in the right triangle on the ground.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — two ships
steps.body:
Near ship: d₁ = 75 cot 45° = 75 m. Far ship: d₂ = 75 cot 30° = 75√3 m.

**Distance between ships = 75(√3 − 1) ≈ 54.9 m**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — building and cable tower
steps.body:
From the top of a 7 m building, the elevation of a cable tower's top is 60° and the depression of its foot is 45°.

Distance = 7 cot 45° = 7 m. Height above building top = 7 tan 60° = 7√3. **Tower = 7 + 7√3 = 7(√3 + 1) ≈ 19.12 m**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — approaching car
steps.body: From a tower, the depression of a car changes from 30° to 60° in 6 s at uniform speed. Distances: h√3 and h/√3. Covered: h√3 − h/√3 = 2h/√3 in 6 s. Remaining: h/√3, which is half of 2h/√3, so it takes **3 s** more.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — two buildings
steps.body: From the top of a 60 m building, the depressions of the top and bottom of a shorter building are 30° and 60°. Distance = 60 cot 60° = 20√3. Difference in heights = 20√3 tan 30° = 20. **Shorter building = 40 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing the angle of depression inside the triangle at the observer from the vertical.
- Adding distances when ships are on the same side (subtract) — add only when they are on opposite sides.
- Mixing up 'height above the building' with the full height.

a.text: From a 100 m cliff, the depressions of two boats on opposite sides of the cliff are 30° and 45°. What do you do first?

choices.label: Find each boat's distance from the cliff foot using cot
Subtract the angles: 45° − 30° = 15°
choices.feedback: Angles cannot be subtracted to get distances. Try again.

b.text: Distances are 100√3 m and 100 m. The boats are on opposite sides, so…

choices.label: Subtract: 100(√3 − 1)
choices.feedback: That is for boats on the same side.

end.text: Distance between boats ≈ 273.2 m. Always read 'same side' or 'opposite sides' carefully!

quiz.q: Distance between the ships in the story:
quiz.why: Both ships are on the same side of the tower, so the distance between them is the difference of the two distances: 75(√3 − 1) m.

quiz.q: Cable tower height in example 2:
quiz.why: The cable tower's height is the sum of the two parts, 7√3... 7 + 7√3 = 7(√3 + 1) m.

quiz.q: Time remaining for the car in example 3:
quiz.why: The car has covered part of the distance in the given time, and the remaining distance is half of that. So the time left is 3 s.

quiz.q: Shorter building in example 4:
quiz.why: The shorter building is 60 − 20 = 40 m.

quiz.q: From a 50 m tower, depression of a car is 45°. Its distance from the foot is
quiz.why: At 45° depression, the distance from the foot equals the height: 50 × cot 45° = 50 m.

questions.why: Horizontal distance = 60 cot 60° = 60/√3 = 20√3 m.

questions.why: At 30° elevation the distance is 60 cot 30° = 60√3 m. It moved 60√3 − 20√3 = 40√3 m.

questions.why: Shadow at 30° is h√3 and at 60° is h/√3. Their difference is h√3 − h/√3 = 2h/√3 = 40, so h = 20√3 m.

questions.why: The depressions equal the angles of elevation from the banks, so the distances are 3 cot 30° = 3√3 and 3 cot 45° = 3. The width is 3√3 + 3 = 3(√3 + 1) m.

questions.why: Height above eye = 87: distances 87/√3 = 29√3 and 87√3; difference 58√3 ≈ 100.46 m.

questions.q: From the top of a 60 m building, depressions of the top and bottom of a tower are 45° and 60°. Tower height:
Elevation of a tower top from points 4 m and 9 m from its base (same line) are complementary. Tower height:
questions.why: For complementary angles tan θ × tan(90° − θ) = 1. So (h/4)(h/9) = 1, giving h² = 36 and h = 6 m.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Circles
courses.summary: Tangents to a circle: why the tangent is perpendicular to the radius, how many tangents a point can have, why tangent lengths from an external point are equal — with both theorem proofs and many board-style applications.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish secants and tangents and state how many tangents pass through a point
Learners can prove that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Learners can prove that tangent lengths from an external point are equal
Learners can solve problems on tangent lengths, concentric circles and circumscribed polygons

scenes.text: When a bicycle wheel rolls on a straight road, it touches the road at exactly one point at each moment.
The road is like a tangent to the circular wheel.
A line that cuts the wheel at two points would be a secant. Today we sort out these lines.

steps.title: Lines and a circle
steps.body:
A line and a circle can have:

- **no** common point (non-intersecting line),
- **two** common points (a **secant**),
- exactly **one** common point (a **tangent**); that point is the **point of contact**.

At any point of a circle there is **exactly one** tangent. A tangent is the limiting position of a secant whose two meeting points come together.

steps.title: How many tangents from a point P?
steps.body:
- P **inside** the circle: none.
- P **on** the circle: exactly one.
- P **outside** the circle: exactly two.

The **length of a tangent** from external P is the distance from P to the point of contact.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — counting
steps.body: How many tangents can a circle have? **Infinitely many** — one at every point. How many parallel to a given secant? **Two** (one on each side).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — tangent length via Pythagoras
steps.body: From Q, 25 cm from the centre O, the tangent length is 24 cm. Since OP ⊥ PQ, r² = 25² − 24² = 625 − 576 = 49 → **r = 7 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a line touching a circle at two points is a tangent (that is a secant).
- Drawing tangents from a point inside the circle.
- Forgetting the right angle at the point of contact when using Pythagoras.

activity.prompt: Match each situation with the number of tangents.
pairs: Tangents a circle can have in total

quiz.q: A line meeting a circle at two points is a
quiz.why: A line meeting a circle at two distinct points is a secant. A tangent meets it at only one point.

quiz.q: Number of tangents from a point outside a circle:
quiz.why: Exactly two tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point outside it.

quiz.q: A tangent to a circle meets it at
quiz.why: A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact.

quiz.q: Tangent from Q (OQ = 25 cm) has length 24 cm. Radius:
quiz.why: The radius is perpendicular to the tangent, so r = √(OQ² − tangent²) = √(625 − 576) = √49 = 7 cm.

quiz.q: The common point of a tangent and the circle is called
quiz.why: The point where a tangent touches the circle is called the point of contact.

scenes.text: An ant at the centre of a round plate wants to walk to a straight ruler lying against the plate's edge.
The shortest path to a line is the perpendicular to it.
The closest point of the ruler is the point of contact — so the radius there must be perpendicular to the ruler.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body: **Theorem:** The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

steps.title: Proof
steps.body:
**Given:** circle with centre O, tangent XY touching at P. **To prove:** OP ⊥ XY.

**Proof:** Take any point Q on XY other than P. Q lies outside the circle (otherwise XY would be a secant). So OQ > radius = OP.

This is true for every Q ≠ P on XY, so OP is the **shortest** distance from O to XY. The shortest segment from a point to a line is perpendicular to it. Hence **OP ⊥ XY** ∎

**Corollary:** the perpendicular to a tangent at its point of contact passes through the centre.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — tangent and radius angle
steps.body: PQ is a tangent at Q to a circle with centre O, and ∠POQ = 60°. Then ∠OQP = 90°, so **∠OPQ = 30°**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — concentric circles
steps.body: Two concentric circles have radii 5 cm and 3 cm. A chord of the larger circle touches the smaller. The radius of the small circle to the point of contact is ⊥ to the chord, so it bisects it: half-chord = √(5² − 3²) = 4. **Chord = 8 cm**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — tangents at ends of a diameter
steps.body: Tangents at the ends A and B of a diameter AB are both perpendicular to AB, so they are **parallel**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the theorem for a chord instead of a tangent.
- Forgetting to say 'Q lies outside the circle' in the proof — that is the key step.
- Assuming the radius bisects a chord without the perpendicular reason.

activity.prompt: Concentric circles have radii 13 cm and 5 cm. Find the length of the chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller one.

quiz.q: The angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact is
quiz.why: The tangent at any point is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact, so the angle is 90°.

quiz.q: Chord of larger concentric circle (radii 5, 3) touching the smaller one:
quiz.why: The radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the chord and bisects it, so half the chord = √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 cm. The full chord is 8 cm.

quiz.q: Tangents at the ends of a diameter are
quiz.why: Both tangents are perpendicular to the same diameter, so they are parallel.

quiz.q: The key idea in the proof of Theorem 1 is that OP is the
options: shortest distance from O to the tangent
quiz.why: The proof uses that OP is the shortest distance from O to the tangent line, because any other point on the tangent is farther. The shortest segment is perpendicular.

quiz.q: If PQ is tangent at Q and ∠POQ = 70°, then ∠OPQ =
quiz.why: The radius OQ is perpendicular to the tangent, so ∠OQP = 90°. In triangle OPQ, ∠OPQ = 180° − 90° − 70° = 20°.

scenes.text: A circus worker ties two ropes from a peg P to a circular tent pole of the big top, each just touching the pole.
Both ropes turn out to be exactly the same length.
That is no coincidence: tangent lengths from an external point are always equal.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body:
**Theorem:** The lengths of the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

Consequences: the tangents are **equally inclined** to the line joining the point to the centre, and the centre lies on the **bisector** of the angle between the tangents.

steps.title: Proof
steps.body:
**Given:** circle centre O, external point P, tangents PQ and PR. **To prove:** PQ = PR.

**Proof:** Join OP, OQ, OR. ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90° (Theorem 1). In right triangles OQP and ORP: OQ = OR (radii), OP is common.

So ΔOQP ≅ ΔORP (**RHS**). Hence **PQ = PR** (CPCT) ∎. Also ∠OPQ = ∠OPR.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — angle between tangents
steps.body:
Tangents PA, PB from P make ∠APB = 80°. In quadrilateral OAPB, ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°, so **∠AOB = 360° − 180° − 80° = 100°**, and ∠POA = 50°.

In general: ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — incircle tangent lengths
steps.body:
A circle is inscribed in ΔABC touching BC, CA, AB at D, E, F. AB = 10, BC = 8, CA = 12. Let AF = AE = x, BF = BD = y, CD = CE = z.

x + y = 10, y + z = 8, z + x = 12 → x + y + z = 15 → **x = 7, y = 3, z = 5**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — circumscribed quadrilateral
steps.body:
A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle. Prove AB + CD = AD + BC.

Let the circle touch AB, BC, CD, DA at P, Q, R, S. Equal tangents: AP = AS, BP = BQ, CR = CQ, DR = DS. Adding: (AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ), i.e. **AB + CD = AD + BC** ∎

So a parallelogram that circumscribes a circle must be a **rhombus**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using SAS instead of RHS in the proof (the right angle and hypotenuse are what we have).
- Assuming the angle between tangents equals the angle at the centre (they are supplementary).
- Pairing the wrong tangent segments at a vertex.

activity.prompt: Tangents PA and PB are drawn from P to a circle with centre O and ∠APB = 70°.

quiz.q: Tangent lengths from an external point are
quiz.why: The lengths of the two tangents from an external point are equal.

quiz.q: The congruence used in proving Theorem 2 is
quiz.why: In triangles OQP and ORP, ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90°, OP is common and OQ = OR. So they are congruent by RHS.

quiz.q: If ∠APB = 80° between tangents, ∠AOB =
quiz.why: In quadrilateral PAOB, ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°, so ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180°. Hence ∠AOB = 180° − 80° = 100°.

quiz.q: A parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a
quiz.why: For a circumscribed parallelogram, AB + CD = AD + BC and opposite sides are equal, so AB = BC. All four sides are equal, so it is a rhombus.

quiz.q: In the incircle example, BD =
quiz.why: Tangents from a vertex are equal, so setting up the equations from the given sides gives BD = 3 in the incircle example.

quiz.q: If PA = 6 cm is a tangent from P, the other tangent PB is
quiz.why: Tangents drawn from the same external point are equal, so PB = PA = 6 cm.

scenes.text: A belt goes around a pulley; the straight parts of the belt are tangents to the wheel.
A mechanic needs angles and lengths to fit a new belt.
Combining both theorems with triangle facts solves a whole family of problems.

steps.title: Toolbox
steps.body:
- Radius ⟂ tangent → right angles → Pythagoras or angle sums.
- Equal tangents → isosceles triangles (PA = PB gives ∠PAB = ∠PBA).
- Angle between tangents + angle at centre = 180°.
- Circumscribed polygon → sums of alternate sides equal.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — prove ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ
steps.body:
TP and TQ are tangents from T to a circle with centre O. Let ∠PTQ = θ. TP = TQ, so ∠TPQ = ∠TQP = (180° − θ)/2 = 90° − θ/2.

∠OPT = 90°, so ∠OPQ = 90° − (90° − θ/2) = θ/2. **Hence ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ** ∎

steps.title: Solved example 2 — tangent length with given angle
steps.body: From P, tangent PA to a circle of radius 5 cm makes ∠APO = 30°. In right ΔOAP, tan 30° = OA/PA → PA = 5√3 cm, and OP = 10 cm (sin 30° = 5/OP).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — triangle circumscribing a circle
steps.body:
ΔABC circumscribes a circle; the circle touches BC at D with BD = 6 cm, DC = 9 cm. If AB = 14 cm, find AC.

BF = BD = 6 → AF = 8 = AE. CE = CD = 9. **AC = 8 + 9 = 17 cm**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — XY ∥ X′Y′
steps.body: Two parallel tangents XY and X′Y′ touch a circle at P and Q; another tangent AB through C meets them at A and B. Then ∠AOB = 90°: OA bisects ∠PAC and OB bisects ∠QBC, and ∠PAB + ∠QBA = 180° (co-interior), so ∠OAB + ∠OBA = 90°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the angle at the centre where the angle at the circumference is needed (Class 9 facts still apply).
- Writing ∠OPQ = θ instead of θ/2.
- Not justifying each equal pair of tangents.

A circle inscribed in a square touches each side at its midpoint.
statements.why: Equal tangents from each vertex split each side equally.

statements.s: Tangent lengths from P depend on which tangent you draw.

quiz.why: In right triangle OAP, tan 30° = OA/AP, so AP = 5/tan 30° = 5√3 cm.

quiz.q: In example 3, AC =
quiz.why: Tangent lengths from the same point are equal, so AC = 8 + 9 = 17 cm.

questions.q: How many tangents can be drawn from a point on a circle?
questions.why: From a point on a circle exactly one tangent can be drawn, the one touching at that point.

questions.q: A tangent is perpendicular to the
options: radius at the point of contact
questions.why: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.

Number of tangents parallel to a given tangent:
questions.why: Only one other tangent is parallel to a given tangent: the one at the opposite end of the diameter through the point of contact.

questions.q: If ∠APB = 50° for tangents PA and PB, ∠AOB =
Assertion: Tangents from an external point are equal. Reason: the two right triangles formed are congruent by RHS.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. The right triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by RHS, so PA = PB, which proves A.

questions.q: Concentric circles of radii 10 cm and 6 cm: chord of the larger touching the smaller is
questions.why: Half the chord = √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8 cm, so the chord is 16 cm.

questions.q: A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle with AB = 5, BC = 8, CD = 7. AD =
questions.why: AB + CD = AD + BC, so 5 + 7 = AD + 8, giving AD = 4.

questions.q: If tangents PA, PB from P are inclined at 80°, then ∠POA =
questions.why: ∠AOB = 180° − 80° = 100°, and OP bisects it, so ∠POA = 50°.

questions.q: Case: A circular garden of radius 14 m touches the four sides of a square path. Length of each side of the square:
questions.why: The circle touches all four sides, so each side equals the diameter, 2 × 14 = 28 m.

questions.q: Case continued: the tangent length from a corner of the square to the garden is
questions.why: The tangent from a corner touches a side at its mid-point, so it is half the side, 28/2 = 14 m.

questions.q: PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm; tangents at P and Q meet at T. The length TP is
questions.why: Distance from O to PQ = 3. Let TR = y (R mid-point): TP² = y² + 16 = (y + 3)² − 25 → 6y = 32 → y = 16/3, TP = √(256/9 + 16) = 20/3.

questions.q: An incircle of ΔABC (right-angled at B, AB = 6, BC = 8) has radius
questions.why: Hypotenuse AC = √(36 + 64) = 10. For a right triangle, r = (AB + BC − AC)/2 = (6 + 8 − 10)/2 = 2.

questions.q: If two tangents from P to a circle of radius r are perpendicular, the tangent length is
questions.why: If the tangents are perpendicular, OAPB has four right angles and OA = OB, so it is a square. The tangent length therefore equals r.

questions.q: The angle between two tangents from a point is 60° and the radius is 4 cm. The distance of the point from the centre is
questions.why: OP bisects the 60° angle, so ∠OPA = 30°. sin 30° = 4/OP gives OP = 8 cm.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Areas Related to Circles
courses.summary: Perimeter and area of a circle revisited, then arc length, area of a sector and area of a segment — applied to clock hands, wipers, lighthouses, brooches and designs, with careful use of π = 22/7 or 3.14.
outcomes: Learners can find circumference and area of circles and use them in reverse
Learners can derive and use arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr and sector area = (θ/360) × πr²
Learners can find minor and major segment areas
Learners can solve real-life sector and segment problems

lessons.title: Circles revisited: circumference and area

scenes.text: A car wheel of diameter 70 cm turns once — how far does the car move?
Exactly one circumference: π × 70 = 220 cm.
And a pizza's size is about area πr². Today we refresh both and use them backwards too.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Circumference = **2πr = πd**
- Area = **πr²**
- π ≈ 22/7 or 3.14 (use the one the question gives).
- Semicircle perimeter = πr + 2r; quadrant area = πr²/4.
- Ring (annulus) area = π(R² − r²).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — wheel revolutions
steps.body: Wheel diameter 70 cm. Distance per revolution = (22/7) × 70 = 220 cm. Revolutions to travel 1.1 km = 110000/220 = **500**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — sum of circles
steps.body:
Find the radius of a circle whose circumference equals the sum of circumferences of circles of radii 19 cm and 9 cm.

2πR = 2π(19) + 2π(9) → **R = 28 cm**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — sum of areas
steps.body:
Find the radius of a circle whose area equals the sum of the areas of circles of radii 8 cm and 6 cm.

πR² = π(64 + 36) → R² = 100 → **R = 10 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding radii when areas are added (areas add as r², not r).
- Using diameter in πr².
- Mixing units (cm and m) in one formula.

activity.prompt: A circular track has circumference 440 m. Find its radius (π = 22/7).

quiz.why: 2πr = πr² gives 2 = r after dividing by πr. So r = 2 units.

quiz.q: Area of a ring with radii 5 and 3 cm:
quiz.why: Area of the ring = π(5² − 3²) = π(25 − 9) = 16π cm².

lessons.title: Arcs and sectors

scenes.text: The minute hand of a wall clock is 14 cm long.
In 5 minutes it turns through 30° and sweeps a pizza-slice shaped region.
That slice is a sector; its curved edge is an arc. Both are fractions θ/360 of the full circle.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
For a sector of angle θ (in degrees) in a circle of radius r:

- **Arc length l = (θ/360°) × 2πr**
- **Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr²** (also = ½ × l × r)
- **Major sector** area = πr² − minor sector area.
- Perimeter of a sector = 2r + l.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — sector of 30°, radius 4 cm (π = 3.14)
Solved example 3 — car wipers
steps.body: Two wipers, blade length 25 cm each, sweep 115°. Total area = 2 × (115/360) × (22/7) × 625 = **1254.96 cm²** (approx.).

steps.title: Solved example 4 — lighthouse warning sector
steps.body: A lighthouse spreads red light over a sector of 80° to a distance of 16.5 km. Area = (80/360) × 3.14 × 16.5² = **189.97 km²** (approx.).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using θ/180 instead of θ/360.
- Forgetting to add 2r when the perimeter of a sector is asked.
- Using the minute hand's 5 minutes as 5°: the hand turns 6° per minute.

activity.label: Slide the sector angle for a circle of radius 7 cm (π = 22/7). Sector area = θ/360 × 154 cm².

bands.text: Small slice: up to 25.7 cm² (60° gives 25.67 cm²).
Most of the circle — a major sector.

quiz.q: Arc length of a 60° sector of radius 21 cm (π = 22/7):
quiz.why: Circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 21 = 132 cm. A 60° sector is 1/6 of it, so the arc is 132/6 = 22 cm.

quiz.q: Area of a quadrant of a circle of radius 14 cm:
quiz.why: Area of the full circle = (22/7) × 14² = 616 cm². A quadrant is 1/4 of it, so 616/4 = 154 cm².

quiz.q: Minute hand of length 14 cm: area swept in 5 min ≈
quiz.why: In 5 minutes the hand turns 30°, which is 1/12 of the circle. 616/12 ≈ 51.33 cm².

quiz.q: The angle turned by a minute hand in 1 minute is
quiz.why: The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, so it turns 360°/60 = 6° each minute.

quiz.q: Sector area can also be written as
quiz.why: Sector area = (θ/360)πr² = ½ × r × [(θ/360) × 2πr] = ½ × l × r, where l is the arc length.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Areas Related to Circles)

lessons.title: Segments of a circle

scenes.text: An arched window is a segment: the region between a chord and its arc.
The builder needs its area to order coloured glass.
Segment = sector minus the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**Minor segment area = sector area − area of ΔOAB**, where O is the centre and AB the chord.

- If θ = 60°, ΔOAB is equilateral: area = (√3/4)r².
- If θ = 90°, ΔOAB is right-angled: area = ½r².
- If θ = 120°, area of ΔOAB = (√3/4)r² (drop a perpendicular from O: height r/2, half-chord (√3/2)r).

**Major segment** = πr² − minor segment.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — chord subtending 60°, r = 21 cm
steps.body:
Sector = (60/360)(22/7)(441) = 231 cm². Triangle (equilateral) = (√3/4)(441) ≈ 190.95 cm².

**Minor segment ≈ 40.05 cm²**. Arc length = (1/6)(2)(22/7)(21) = 22 cm.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — right angle, r = 10 cm (π = 3.14)
steps.body: Sector = 78.5 cm², triangle = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 cm². **Minor segment = 28.5 cm²; major segment = 314 − 28.5 = 285.5 cm²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to subtract the triangle (giving the sector instead of the segment).
- Using ½ × base × height with the radius as height for non-right triangles.
- Mixing π values within one problem.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the area of a minor segment.
items: Note r and the angle θ at the centre
Find the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord
For the major segment, subtract the minor segment from πr²

quiz.q: A segment is the region between
quiz.why: A segment of a circle is the region between a chord and the arc it cuts off. A sector lies between two radii and an arc.

quiz.q: Minor segment for θ = 90°, r = 10 cm (π = 3.14):
quiz.why: Sector area = (90/360) × 3.14 × 100 = 78.5 cm². Triangle OAB = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 cm². Minor segment = 78.5 − 50 = 28.5 cm².

quiz.q: Area of triangle OAB when θ = 60° and r = 6 cm:
quiz.why: With θ = 60° and OA = OB = 6, the triangle is equilateral with side 6. Area = (√3/4) × 6² = 9√3 cm².

quiz.q: Major segment area =
quiz.why: The major segment is the rest of the circle after removing the minor segment, so its area = πr² − area of minor segment.

quiz.q: For θ = 120°, the triangle OAB has area
quiz.why: Area of triangle OAB = ½ r² sin θ = ½ r² sin 120° = ½ r² × √3/2 = (√3/4)r².

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Areas Related to Circles)

lessons.title: Designs and applications

scenes.text: A craftsman makes a circular brooch of diameter 35 mm from silver wire, with 5 diameters dividing it into 10 equal sectors.
How much wire? What is the area of each sector?
Design questions combine circumference, arcs and sectors.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Break the design into circles, sectors, segments, triangles and rectangles. Add the pieces you keep and subtract the pieces cut out. Keep exact π until the last step if possible.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — umbrella panels
steps.body: An umbrella has 8 equally spaced ribs; treat it as a flat circle of radius 45 cm. Area between two consecutive ribs = (1/8)(22/7)(2025) = **795.54 cm²** (approx.).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — grazing horse
steps.body: A horse is tied to a corner peg of a square field of side 15 m with a 5 m rope. Grazing area = quadrant = (1/4)(3.14)(25) = **19.625 m²**. With a 10 m rope: (1/4)(3.14)(100) = 78.5 m², an increase of **58.875 m²**.

steps.title: Where it shows up
steps.body: Fan blade sweep, sprinkler coverage, pizza slice pricing, race-track lanes, rangoli designs, the area a wiper cleans, and radar/lighthouse coverage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the extra straight pieces (diameters/radii) in wire problems.
- Treating a rope tied at a corner as a semicircle (it is a quadrant when the angle is 90°).
- Rounding intermediate values heavily.

activity.prompt: A sprinkler waters a sector of angle 90° and radius 14 m. Watered area? (π = 22/7)

quiz.q: Brooch wire length in the story:
quiz.why: The wire length in the brooch is the sum of the two parts: 110 mm + 175 mm = 285 mm.

quiz.q: Area grazed by a horse tied at a corner of a square field with a 7 m rope (π = 22/7):
quiz.why: A horse tied at the corner of a square field can graze a quarter circle. Area = ¼ × (22/7) × 7² = ¼ × 154 = 38.5 m².

quiz.q: Perimeter of a semicircular protractor of diameter 14 cm:
quiz.why: Perimeter = semicircle arc + diameter = πr + 2r = 22 + 14 = 36 cm, with r = 7 cm.

quiz.q: Each of 10 equal sectors of a circle of radius 7 cm has area
quiz.why: The circle's area is (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm². Ten equal sectors share it equally, so each has 154/10 = 15.4 cm².

quiz.q: Increase in grazing area when the rope grows from 5 m to 10 m (corner, π = 3.14):
quiz.why: Quadrant areas: ¼ × 3.14 × 100 = 78.5 m² (10 m) and ¼ × 3.14 × 25 = 19.625 m² (5 m). The increase is 78.5 − 19.625 = 58.875 m².

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Areas Related to Circles)

questions.q: Area of a circle of radius 14 cm (π = 22/7):
Area of a sector of angle θ is
questions.why: A sector of angle θ is the fraction θ/360 of the whole circle, so its area is (θ/360) × πr².

questions.q: Arc length of a semicircle of radius 7 cm:
questions.why: The arc of a semicircle is half the circumference: πr = (22/7) × 7 = 22 cm.

questions.q: If the perimeter and area of a circle are numerically equal, the radius is
questions.why: 2πr = πr² gives r = 2 after dividing both sides by πr.

questions.q: Area of a quadrant of a circle with circumference 22 cm:
questions.why: Circumference 22 = 2πr gives r = 7/2. Quadrant area = ¼ × (22/7) × (49/4) = 77/8 cm².

questions.q: Assertion: The area of a sector of 90° is one-quarter of the circle. Reason: 90/360 = 1/4.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A 90° sector is 90/360 = 1/4 of the circle, so both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at the centre. Minor segment area (π = 3.14):
questions.why: Sector = ¼ × 3.14 × 100 = 78.5 cm² and triangle = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 cm². Minor segment = 78.5 − 50 = 28.5 cm².

questions.q: The length of the minute hand is 7 cm. Area swept in 15 minutes (π = 22/7):
questions.why: In 15 minutes the minute hand turns 90°, a quarter circle. Area = ¼ × (22/7) × 49 = 38.5 cm².

questions.q: Case: A pizza of diameter 28 cm is cut into 8 equal slices. Area of each slice (π = 22/7):
questions.why: The pizza has r = 14 cm, so its area is (22/7) × 196 = 616 cm². Each of 8 equal slices has 616/8 = 77 cm².

questions.q: Case continued: the crust length (arc) of each slice is
questions.why: Circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 14 = 88 cm. Each of the 8 slices has an arc of 88/8 = 11 cm.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 0.35 m makes how many revolutions to cover 1.1 km? (π = 22/7)
questions.why: Circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 0.35 = 2.2 m. Revolutions = 1100 m ÷ 2.2 m = 500.

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 12 cm subtends 120°. Segment area (π = 3.14, √3 = 1.73):
Area of the region between a square of side 14 cm and the largest circle inside it (π = 22/7):
questions.why: The largest circle in a square of side 14 has r = 7, so area 154 cm². The square is 196 cm², so the leftover region is 196 − 154 = 42 cm².

questions.q: Two circles touch internally; the sum of their areas is 116π cm² and the distance between centres is 6 cm. Their radii are
questions.why: Touching internally gives R − r = 6, and R² + r² = 116 (π cancels). Trying R = 10, r = 4: 10 − 4 = 6 and 100 + 16 = 116.

questions.q: A sector of a circle of radius 21 cm has perimeter 64 cm. Its area is
questions.why: Perimeter = 2r + arc, so arc = 64 − 42 = 22 cm. Area = ½ × arc × r = ½ × 22 × 21 = 231 cm².

courses.title: Ch 12 · Surface Areas and Volumes
courses.summary: Surface areas and volumes of solids made by combining cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres and hemispheres — toys, capsules, tents, pen stands and sweets — with every formula and step shown.
outcomes: Learners can recall CSA, TSA and volume formulas of the basic solids
Learners can decide which surfaces are visible when solids are joined
Learners can find surface areas of combined solids
Learners can find volumes of combined and hollowed solids
Learners can solve cost and capacity problems

lessons.title: The formula toolkit

scenes.text: Lata's kitchen has a tin (cylinder), an ice-cream cone, a ball of dough (sphere) and a bowl (hemisphere).
To wrap or fill each one, she needs surface area or volume.
Before combining solids, let us lay out every formula once, neatly.

steps.title: Formula sheet (r radius, h height, l slant height)
steps.body:
- **Cuboid:** TSA = 2(lb + bh + hl), V = lbh
- **Cube (side a):** TSA = 6a², V = a³
- **Cylinder:** CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r + h), V = πr²h
- **Cone:** l = √(r² + h²), CSA = πrl, TSA = πr(l + r), V = ⅓πr²h
- **Sphere:** SA = 4πr², V = (4/3)πr³
- **Hemisphere:** CSA = 2πr², TSA = 3πr², V = (2/3)πr³

steps.title: Solved example 2 — hemisphere bowl
steps.body: Inner radius 10.5 cm. Capacity = (2/3)(22/7)(10.5)³ = **2425.5 cm³** ≈ 2.43 litres (1000 cm³ = 1 L).

steps.title: Units
steps.body: Areas in square units, volumes in cubic units. 1 m³ = 1000 L; 1 L = 1000 cm³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the height h instead of slant height l in πrl.
- Using 3πr² (hemisphere TSA) when only the curved surface is exposed.
- Forgetting to convert diameter to radius.

activity.prompt: Match each solid with its volume formula.

quiz.q: CSA of a cone is
quiz.why: The curved surface area of a cone is πrl, where l is the slant height. πr(l + r) is the total surface area, which includes the base.

quiz.q: Slant height of a cone with r = 6, h = 8:
Volume of a sphere of radius 3 cm:
quiz.why: Volume = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π × 27 = 36π cm³.

quiz.q: TSA of a solid hemisphere of radius r:
quiz.why: A solid hemisphere has a curved surface of 2πr² and a flat circular base of πr², so TSA = 3πr².

quiz.q: 1 m³ equals
quiz.why: 1 m³ = 100 × 100 × 100 cm³ = 10,00,000 cm³, and 1 litre = 1000 cm³, so 1 m³ = 1000 litres.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Surface Areas and Volumes)

lessons.title: Surface area of combined solids

scenes.text: Rasika has a toy: a cone sitting on a hemisphere, both of radius 3.5 cm, total height 5 cm.
She wants to paint it. Which surfaces get paint?
Only the outside: the cone's curved surface and the hemisphere's curved surface. The joined circles are hidden.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: When solids are joined, the **surface area of the combination = sum of the exposed surfaces**. Joined faces are hidden and must not be counted. Often: TSA = CSA of part 1 + CSA of part 2 (+ any exposed flat faces).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — cube with hemisphere on top
steps.body: Cube side 7 cm, hemisphere of diameter 7 cm on top. Exposed = cube TSA − circle (covered) + hemisphere CSA = 6(49) − πr² + 2πr² = 294 + πr² = 294 + 38.5 = **332.5 cm²**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — capsule
steps.body:
A capsule is a cylinder with two hemispherical ends: total length 14 mm, diameter 5 mm. r = 2.5, cylinder length = 14 − 5 = 9 mm.

SA = 2πrh + 4πr² = 2π(2.5)(9) + 4π(6.25) = 45π + 25π = 70π = **220 mm²**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — tent canvas
steps.body: A tent is a cylinder (height 2.1 m, diameter 4 m) topped by a cone of slant height 2.8 m. Canvas = 2πrh + πrl = 2(22/7)(2)(2.1) + (22/7)(2)(2.8) = 26.4 + 17.6 = **44 m²**. At ₹500/m², cost = ₹22,000. (The floor is not covered.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding the TSA of both solids (counts hidden faces twice).
- Forgetting the flat ring/circle that remains exposed (cube top minus hemisphere base).
- Using total length as the cylinder length in a capsule.

activity.prompt: For a cone on top of a cylinder (toy), which surfaces are painted?

quiz.q: Capsule surface area in the example:
quiz.why: The capsule's surface is made of a cylinder's curved part and two hemispheres. Putting in the given measurements gives 70π ≈ 220 mm².

quiz.q: For a cube with a hemisphere on top, the extra area beyond the cube's TSA is
quiz.why: A hemisphere on a cube hides a circle (πr²) of the cube's top but adds a curved surface of 2πr². The net change is −πr² + 2πr² = πr².

quiz.q: Tent canvas area in the example:
quiz.why: The tent canvas is the cylinder's curved area plus the cone's curved area: 26.4 + 17.6 = 44 m².

quiz.q: Combined solids' surface area counts
quiz.why: For combined solids, only exposed surfaces are counted. Faces where the solids join are hidden and left out.

quiz.q: A wooden article is a cylinder (h = 10, r = 3.5) with a hemisphere scooped out of each end. Its TSA is
quiz.why: The TSA is the cylinder's curved area plus the inner curved areas of two hemispheres: 2πrh + 4πr² = 220 + 154 = 374 cm².

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Surface Areas and Volumes)

lessons.title: Volume of combined solids

scenes.text: A sweet shop makes 45 gulab jamuns, each shaped like a cylinder with two hemispherical ends, 5 cm long and 2.8 cm across.
Each contains syrup equal to 30% of its volume.
Volumes simply add (or subtract for hollows) — no hidden-face worry here.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: **Volume of a combination = sum of volumes of the parts.** For a solid with a hole or scoop, **subtract** the removed volume.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — pen stand
steps.body:
A cuboid 15 cm × 10 cm × 3.5 cm has four conical depressions, each radius 0.5 cm, depth 1.4 cm.

Wood = 525 − 4 × ⅓(22/7)(0.25)(1.4) = 525 − 1.47 = **523.53 cm³**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — cone on hemisphere
steps.body: Radius 1 cm, cone height 1 cm. V = (2/3)π(1)³ + ⅓π(1)²(1) = π ≈ **3.14 cm³**.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — vessel
steps.body:
A vessel is a hemispherical bowl of radius 7 cm topped by a cylinder of the same radius, total height 13 cm. Cylinder height = 6 cm.

V = (2/3)(22/7)(343) + (22/7)(49)(6) = 718.67 + 924 = **1642.67 cm³** (approx.).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting surface areas when volumes are needed.
- Using total height of the vessel for the cylinder part.
- Forgetting to multiply by the number of objects.

activity.prompt: A solid is a cylinder (r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm) with a cone of the same radius and height 6 cm on top. Find its volume (π = 22/7).

quiz.q: Volume of cone on hemisphere (r = h = 1 cm):
quiz.why: Hemisphere = (2/3)π(1)³ = 2π/3 and cone = (1/3)π(1)²(1) = π/3. Together they give π cm³.

quiz.q: Pen stand wood volume ≈
quiz.why: Volume of the wood = volume of the cuboid minus the volumes of the depressions scooped out. That works out to about 523.53 cm³.

quiz.q: Volume of a combined solid is found by
quiz.why: The volume of a combined solid is the sum of the volumes of its parts. Surface areas do not simply add.

quiz.q: A cylinder with a cone scooped out (same r and h) has remaining volume
quiz.why: Cylinder πr²h minus cone (1/3)πr²h leaves (2/3)πr²h.

quiz.q: Syrup in 45 gulab jamuns ≈
quiz.why: The syrup is 30% of the total volume of the gulab jamuns, which is about 0.3 × 1127.4 ≈ 338 cm³.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Surface Areas and Volumes)

lessons.title: Problem solving: cost, capacity and design

story.title: The water tank on the roof

scenes.text: A building's tank is a cylinder with a hemispherical bottom.
The plumber needs its capacity; the painter needs its outer area.
Real problems ask both — read carefully which one is wanted.

steps.title: Checklist for any problem
steps.body:
1. Sketch and label each part with r, h, l.
2. Decide: **area** (painting, wrapping, canvas, polishing) or **volume** (capacity, material, liquid)?
3. For area: list exposed surfaces only. For volume: add or subtract parts.
4. Convert units and compute cost = area × rate (or volume × rate).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — birdbath
steps.body: A birdbath is a cylinder (h = 1.45 m, r = 30 cm) with a hemispherical depression at the top. Outer + inner surface: 2πrh + 2πr² = 2π(0.3)(1.45 + 0.3) = 2(22/7)(0.3)(1.75) = **3.3 m²**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — cost of polishing
steps.body: A wooden article is a cylinder 10 cm tall, r = 3.5 cm, with hemispherical scoops at both ends is polished at ₹0.10 per cm². Area = 374 cm² (from the earlier lesson). **Cost = ₹37.40**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — ice-cream in cones
steps.body: A cylinder of ice-cream (r = 6 cm, h = 15 cm) is filled into cones of radius 3 cm and height 12 cm topped with a hemisphere. Each cone holds ⅓π(9)(12) + (2/3)π(27) = 36π + 18π = 54π. Cylinder = π(36)(15) = 540π. **Number of cones = 10**.

steps.title: Everyday uses
steps.body: Paint needed for water tanks, cloth for tents, metal for pipes, number of bricks for a wall, capacity of a pressure cooker or a petrol tanker — all use these formulas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Answering capacity in cm³ when litres are asked.
- Forgetting that a hollow (open) object has no top face to paint.
- Computing cost with area in cm² but rate per m².

activity.prompt: Before writing your final answer, check that you:
items: Converted all lengths to the same unit
Counted only exposed surfaces for area
Rounded only at the last step

quiz.q: Painting a tank asks for
quiz.why: Painting covers the outside of the tank, so we need surface area, not volume.

quiz.q: Birdbath total area in the example:
quiz.why: The birdbath is a cylinder with a hemisphere's surface, giving total area 2πr(h + r), which comes to 3.3 m² for the given values.

quiz.q: Number of ice-cream cones in example 3:
quiz.why: Volume of the cylinder ÷ volume of one cone = 540π ÷ 54π = 10 cones.

quiz.q: 1 litre equals
quiz.why: Conversion.

quiz.q: Cost of polishing 374 cm² at ₹0.10 per cm²:

sources: NCERT Class 10 Mathematics (Surface Areas and Volumes)

questions.q: Volume of a cylinder is
questions.why: The volume of a cylinder is πr²h, the base area times height.

questions.q: CSA of a hemisphere of radius 7 cm (π = 22/7):
questions.why: Curved surface area of a hemisphere = 2πr² = 2 × (22/7) × 49 = 308 cm².

questions.q: A cone and a cylinder have the same r and h. Ratio of their volumes is
questions.why: Cone volume = (1/3)πr²h and cylinder volume = πr²h, so the ratio is 1 : 3.

questions.q: Surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm:
questions.why: Surface area = 4πr² = 4 × (22/7) × 49 = 616 cm².

questions.q: Two cubes of side 4 cm are joined end to end. TSA of the cuboid formed:
questions.why: Joined end to end, the cubes form a cuboid 8 × 4 × 4. TSA = 2(32 + 16 + 32) = 160 cm².

questions.q: Assertion: When two solids are joined, the TSA of the combination is the sum of their TSAs. Reason: Joined faces become hidden.
questions.why: When solids are joined, the faces that touch are hidden, so they are not part of the TSA. Hence A is false and R is true.

questions.q: A toy is a cone of radius 3.5 cm on a hemisphere of the same radius. Total height 15.5 cm. Its TSA (π = 22/7):
questions.why: The cone has height 15.5 − 3.5 = 12, so slant height l = √(3.5² + 12²) = 12.5. TSA = πrl + 2πr² = 11 × (12.5 + 7) = 11 × 19.5 = 214.5 cm².

questions.q: Volume of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm:
questions.why: Volume of a hemisphere = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π × 27 = 18π cm³.

questions.q: Case: A juice seller uses a cylindrical glass of inner diameter 5 cm and height 10 cm, but its bottom has a raised hemisphere of radius 2.5 cm. Apparent capacity (π = 3.14):
questions.why: The apparent capacity ignores the raised hemisphere: π × 2.5² × 10 = 3.14 × 6.25 × 10 = 196.25 cm³.

questions.q: Case continued: actual capacity of the glass:
questions.why: The raised hemisphere takes up (2/3)(3.14)(15.625) = 32.71 cm³. Actual capacity = 196.25 − 32.71 = 163.54 cm³.

questions.q: A solid cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 5 cm has a cone of the same base and height 4 cm on top. Volume:
questions.why: The cylinder is π × 9 × 5 = 45π and the cone is (1/3)π × 9 × 4 = 12π. Total = 57π cm³.

questions.q: A medicine capsule is 14 mm long with diameter 5 mm. Its volume (π = 22/7) approximately:
questions.why: The capsule is a cylinder of length 14 − 5 = 9 mm and radius 2.5 plus a sphere. Volume ≈ 176.8 + 65.5 = 242.3 mm³.

questions.q: A hemispherical tank of radius 1.75 m is full of water. Water in kL (π = 22/7) is about
questions.why: Volume = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)(22/7)(1.75³) ≈ 11.23 m³. Since 1 m³ = 1 kL, the water is about 11.23 kL.

questions.q: A cylinder of radius 6 cm and height 15 cm of ice-cream fills cones (r = 3, h = 12, with hemispherical tops). Number of cones:
questions.why: Ice-cream in the cylinder is π × 36 × 15 = 540π. Each cone with its hemispherical top holds 36π + 18π = 54π, so 540π ÷ 54π = 10 cones.

questions.q: A cube of side 10 cm has the largest possible sphere carved out of it. Remaining volume (π = 3.14):
questions.why: The largest sphere has r = 5, so volume = (4/3)(3.14)(125) = 523.33 cm³. Remaining = 1000 − 523.33 = 476.67 cm³.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Statistics
courses.summary: Mean, mode and median of grouped data: the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods for the mean, the modal-class formula, cumulative frequency and the median formula, and how the three measures relate.
outcomes: Learners can find the mean of grouped data by three methods
Learners can find the mode of grouped data with the modal-class formula
Learners can build a cumulative frequency table and find the median
Learners can find a missing frequency from a given mean or median
Learners can use the empirical relation 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean

scenes.text: Mrs Iyer has the marks of 50 students grouped as 0–10, 10–20, …, 40–50.
She does not know each exact mark — only how many fall in each class.
Using the class mark (mid-point) of each class as its representative, she can still find the mean.

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body:
**Class mark** xᵢ = (lower limit + upper limit)/2.

- **Direct:** x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ
- **Assumed mean:** choose a (a middle class mark), dᵢ = xᵢ − a, x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ/Σfᵢ
- **Step deviation:** uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h (h = class width), **x̄ = a + h × Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ**

All three give the same answer; step deviation keeps numbers small.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — step deviation on the same data
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using class limits instead of class marks.
- Forgetting to multiply by h in the step-deviation formula.
- Signs of uᵢ below a (they are negative).

activity.prompt: Find the mean: classes 0–4, 4–8, 8–12 with frequencies 2, 3, 5.

quiz.q: Class mark of 20–30 is
quiz.why: Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2 = (20 + 30)/2 = 25.

quiz.q: Mean in example 1 is
In the step-deviation method, uᵢ =
quiz.why: In the step-deviation method, uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h, where a is the assumed mean and h the class width.

quiz.q: Mean of daily wages in example 3:
quiz.why: By the step-deviation method, mean = a + h × (Σfu/Σf) = 150 − 1.6 = ₹148.40.

quiz.q: If Σfᵢ = 40 and Σfᵢxᵢ = 1000, mean =

scenes.text: A survey of 30 households records family size in classes 1–3, 3–5, 5–7, 7–9, 9–11.
The class 3–5 has the most families, but the exact 'most common size' is somewhere inside it.
A formula estimates where inside the modal class the peak lies.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**Modal class** = class with the highest frequency.

**Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h**

- l = lower limit of modal class, h = class width
- f₁ = frequency of modal class, f₀ = of the class before, f₂ = of the class after.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — test marks (data of lesson 1)
Solved example 3 — first class is modal
steps.body: If the first class is modal, take f₀ = 0. If the last class is modal, take f₂ = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the highest class mark instead of the highest frequency.
- Taking f₀ and f₂ from the wrong neighbours.
- Writing the denominator as f₁ − f₀ − f₂ instead of 2f₁ − f₀ − f₂.

Cumulative frequencies tell us which class holds the middle, and a formula pins it down.

steps.title: Formula

2. Find n/2. The **median class** is the first class whose cf ≥ n/2.
3. **Median = l + [(n/2 − cf)/f] × h**

l = lower limit of median class, cf = cumulative frequency of the class **before** it, f = frequency of the median class, h = class width.

lessons.title: Choosing a measure and the empirical relation

scenes.text: A housing society's incomes include a few very rich families.
The mean is pulled up by them; the median shows the typical family better; the mode shows the most common income.
Knowing which measure fits the question is part of the exam too.

steps.title: Which one when?
steps.body:
- **Mean:** uses every value; good for comparing totals and averages (e.g. average marks of two sections). Sensitive to extreme values.
- **Median:** the middle value; best when data are skewed (incomes, house prices).
- **Mode:** the most frequent value; best for 'most popular' questions (shoe size, family size).

**Empirical relation** (for moderately skewed data): **3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — use the relation
steps.body: If mean = 27 and median = 28, then mode ≈ 3(28) − 2(27) = 84 − 54 = **30**. (The formula in lesson 2 gave 30.91 — close, as expected for an approximate relation.)

steps.title: Solved example 3 — choose a measure
steps.body: (a) A shoe shop restocks the most popular size → **mode**. (b) Typical salary in a company with a highly paid CEO → **median**. (c) Average rainfall over a year → **mean**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the empirical relation as exact.
- Writing 3 Mean = Mode + 2 Median (wrong placement).
- Using the mean for heavily skewed data without comment.

courses.title: Ch 14 · Probability
courses.summary: Theoretical probability of equally likely outcomes: sure and impossible events, complementary events, and full sample spaces for coins, dice, cards, balls, numbered discs and real-life cases.
outcomes: Learners can define outcome, event and theoretical probability
Learners can use 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1 and P(E) + P(not E) = 1
Learners can list sample spaces for one or more coins and two dice
Learners can solve card, ball, disc and defective-item problems
Learners can avoid common counting errors

scenes.text: Before a match, the captain calls 'Heads!' as the coin spins.
Two outcomes are equally likely, and one of them is a win for the call.
So the chance is 1 out of 2. Probability turns 'chance' into a number between 0 and 1.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Experiment:** an action with well-defined outcomes (tossing a coin).
- **Outcome:** a possible result; **sample space:** all outcomes.
- **Event:** a collection of outcomes (getting an even number).
- If outcomes are **equally likely**, **P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (total number of outcomes)**.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
- 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1.
- **Sure event:** P = 1. **Impossible event:** P = 0.
- **Complement:** P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
- An event with only one outcome is an **elementary event**; the probabilities of all elementary events add to 1.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — one die
steps.body: P(getting a number greater than 4) = favourable {5, 6} / 6 = **1/3**. P(not greater than 4) = 1 − 1/3 = **2/3**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — sure and impossible
steps.body: With one die: P(number less than 7) = 6/6 = **1** (sure). P(getting 8) = 0/6 = **0** (impossible).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — complement
steps.body: If P(rain tomorrow) = 0.35, then P(no rain) = **0.65**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a probability greater than 1 or negative.
- Treating outcomes as equally likely when they are not (e.g. 'win, lose or draw' in a match are not automatically 1/3 each).
- Forgetting to simplify fractions.

statements.s: A probability can be 1.2.
P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
Getting 7 on a normal die is an impossible event.
The outcomes 'win', 'lose', 'draw' are always equally likely.
The probability of a sure event is 1.

quiz.why: An impossible event has no favourable outcomes, so its probability is 0.

quiz.why: A probability lies between 0 and 1, so a negative number like −1.5 cannot be a probability.

scenes.text: Zoya and Aman play Ludo with two dice and argue about which sum comes most often.
Aman lists all 36 ordered pairs (1,1) to (6,6).
Sum 7 appears 6 times — more than any other. Listing the sample space settles arguments.

steps.title: Sample spaces
steps.body:
- **Two coins:** HH, HT, TH, TT (4 outcomes).
- **Three coins:** HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT (8).
- **Two dice:** 6 × 6 = **36** ordered pairs. (1, 2) and (2, 1) are **different** outcomes.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — two coins
steps.body: P(at least one head) = {HH, HT, TH}/4 = **3/4**. P(exactly one head) = 2/4 = **1/2**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — sum 8 with two dice
Solved example 4 — three coins
steps.body: P(exactly two heads) = {HHT, HTH, THH}/8 = **3/8**. P(at least two heads) = 4/8 = **1/2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting (1, 2) and (2, 1) as one outcome — that makes outcomes unequal in likelihood.
- Listing 3 outcomes for two coins ('two heads, two tails, one each') — 'one each' is twice as likely.
- Forgetting doublets like (4, 4).

scenes.text: A magician shuffles a 52-card deck and asks Neel to pick one.
Neel wonders how likely he is to get a red king, a face card or a spade.
Knowing the deck's structure makes these easy.

steps.title: A deck of 52 cards
steps.body:
- 4 suits: ♠ spades, ♣ clubs (black); ♥ hearts, ♦ diamonds (red) — 13 cards each.
- Each suit: A, 2–10, J, Q, K.
- **Face cards:** J, Q, K → 12 in all. Aces: 4. Kings: 4 (2 red, 2 black).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — balls in a bag
steps.body:
A bag has 3 red and 5 black balls. P(red) = 3/8, P(not red) = **5/8**.

If it has 5 red, 8 white and 4 green: P(not green) = 13/17.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — defective items
steps.body: Of 144 ball pens, 20 are defective. P(a pen is good) = 124/144 = **31/36**.

steps.title: Solved example 5 — find a number from a probability
steps.body: A box has 12 balls, x of them black. P(black) = x/12. If 6 more black balls are added, P doubles: (x + 6)/18 = 2x/12 → 12x + 72 = 36x → **x = 3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting aces as face cards (they are not).
- Forgetting that 'red' includes both hearts and diamonds.
- Using 100 as the total when discs are numbered 1–90.

scenes.text: A school fair sells 1000 tickets; there are 5 prizes.
Ravi buys one ticket. His friend buys ten.
Ravi's chance is 5/1000 = 1/200. Real problems use the same counting — just read carefully.

steps.title: Reading a case
steps.body:
1. Identify the experiment and the **total** equally likely outcomes.
2. Identify the favourable outcomes — list them if small.
3. Use complements for 'at least' or 'not' questions.
4. Simplify and sanity-check (0 ≤ P ≤ 1).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — lottery
steps.body: P(Ravi wins a prize) = 5/1000 = **1/200**. P(not winning) = **199/200**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — leap year
steps.body: A non-leap year has 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 day, so P(53 Sundays) = 1/7. A leap year has 52 weeks + 2 days; the extra pair is one of 7 possibilities (Sun–Mon, Mon–Tue, … , Sat–Sun), 2 contain Sunday → **2/7**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — game of chance
steps.body: A spinning arrow can stop at 1, 2, …, 8 equally likely. P(odd) = 4/8 = 1/2; P(number > 2) = 6/8 = 3/4; P(number < 9) = 1.

steps.title: Solved example 4 — two-player meeting days
steps.body: Two customers each visit a shop on one day from Tuesday to Saturday (5 days), equally likely. P(same day) = 5/25 = **1/5**; P(consecutive days) = 8/25; P(different days) = **4/5**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming a leap year has 53 Sundays for sure.
- Using 5 instead of 25 as the total for two independent choices.
- Forgetting order: (Tue, Wed) and (Wed, Tue) are different outcomes.

lessons.title: Formula sheet I: Number systems and algebra (Ch 1–5)

scenes.text: The night before the exam, Kavya wants all algebra formulas on one page.
She writes them from memory, then checks them here.
Self-testing beats rereading. Try covering each box and recalling it.

steps.title: Real numbers
steps.body:
- FTA: every composite = unique product of primes.
- HCF = product of smallest powers of common primes; LCM = product of greatest powers of all primes.
- HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b (two numbers only).
- √p is irrational for prime p; rational ± irrational is irrational.

steps.title: Polynomials
steps.body:
- ax² + bx + c: α + β = −b/a, αβ = c/a.
- Quadratic from zeroes: k[x² − (α + β)x + αβ].
- α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ.
- Cubic: Σα = −b/a, Σαβ = c/a, αβγ = −d/a.

steps.title: Linear equations
steps.body:
- a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ → unique; a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ → infinitely many; a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ → none.
- Methods: graphical, substitution, elimination.

steps.title: Quadratic equations
steps.body:
- x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/2a.
- D = b² − 4ac: D > 0 two distinct, D = 0 equal (−b/2a), D < 0 no real roots.

steps.title: Arithmetic progressions
steps.body:
- aₙ = a + (n − 1)d; nth from end = l − (n − 1)d.
- Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d] = n/2(a + l); aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁.
- 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2; first n odd numbers sum to n².

steps.title: Top 4 algebra slips
steps.body:
- Sign of −b/a.
- HCF × LCM rule for three numbers.
- a + nd instead of a + (n − 1)d.
- Forgetting to check the c-ratio.

lessons.title: Formula sheet II: Geometry and trigonometry (Ch 6–10)

scenes.text: Rohit can never remember which side is 'opposite'.
He draws a tiny right triangle in the margin for every trig question.
Quick sketches turn formulas into pictures — and pictures are hard to forget.

steps.title: Triangles
steps.body:
- Similar: equal angles AND proportional sides.
- BPT: DE ∥ BC ⇒ AD/DB = AE/EC; converse holds.
- Criteria: AA, SSS, SAS (included angle).

steps.title: Coordinate geometry
steps.body:
- Distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
- Section (m₁ : m₂): ((m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂)).
- Mid-point: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). Centroid: average of three vertices.

steps.title: Trigonometry
steps.body:
- sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj; reciprocals cosec, sec, cot.
- sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = 1/√2, sin 60° = √3/2 (cos runs backwards); tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3.
- sin² + cos² = 1; 1 + tan² = sec²; 1 + cot² = cosec².

steps.title: Heights and distances
steps.body:
- Angle of depression from A to B = angle of elevation from B to A.
- Use tan for height–distance; sin/cos when a slant length (ladder, string) is involved.
- √3 ≈ 1.732, √2 ≈ 1.414.

steps.title: Circles
steps.body:
- Tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact.
- Tangents from an external point are equal.
- Angle between tangents + angle at centre = 180°.
- Circumscribed quadrilateral: AB + CD = AD + BC.

steps.title: Top 4 geometry slips
steps.body:
- Wrong vertex order in similarity.
- m₁ paired with x₁ in the section formula.
- sin(A + B) ≠ sin A + sin B.
- Same side vs opposite sides in ship problems.

scenes.text: These chapters carry many marks and are mostly formula-and-calculation.
Careful arithmetic matters more than tricks.
Revise formulas, then practise one problem of each type.

steps.title: Areas related to circles
steps.body:
- C = 2πr, A = πr².
- Arc = (θ/360) 2πr; sector = (θ/360) πr² = ½lr.
- Minor segment = sector − ΔOAB (60°: (√3/4)r²; 90°: ½r²).

steps.title: Surface areas and volumes
steps.body:
- Cylinder: CSA 2πrh, V πr²h. Cone: l = √(r² + h²), CSA πrl, V ⅓πr²h.
- Sphere: 4πr², (4/3)πr³. Hemisphere: CSA 2πr², TSA 3πr², V (2/3)πr³.
- Combined: area = exposed surfaces only; volume = sum (or difference).

steps.title: Statistics
steps.body:
- Mean: x̄ = a + h Σfu/Σf.
- Mode: l + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × h.
- Median: l + (n/2 − cf)/f × h.
- 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean.

steps.title: Probability
steps.body:
- P(E) = favourable/total (equally likely).
- 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
- Two dice: 36 outcomes; three coins: 8; deck: 52 cards, 12 face cards.

steps.title: Exam-day strategy
steps.body:
- Read all questions in the first 10–15 minutes; start with what you know best.
- Show steps: formula → substitution → answer with units.
- For case-based questions, read the case twice.
- Leave 10 minutes to check signs, units and calculations.
