lessons.title: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants

story.title: The bee and the mustard field

scenes.text: In a mustard field, bees move from flower to flower, dusted with yellow pollen.
Pollen reaching the right flower starts a journey that ends in seeds.
Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents, creating more variation.

steps.title: Why sexual reproduction?
steps.body:
Two **germ cells** (gametes) fuse. Each germ cell has **half** the DNA (one set of chromosomes), so the zygote gets the full amount. Mixing DNA from two individuals creates **new combinations of variations**.

Germ cells are specialised: one is often larger with food stores (female), the other smaller and motile (male).

steps.title: Flower to seed
steps.body:
- **Flower parts:** sepals, petals, **stamens** (male; anther makes pollen) and **pistil/carpel** (female; stigma, style, ovary with ovules).
- **Unisexual** flowers have either stamens or pistil (papaya, watermelon); **bisexual** have both (Hibiscus, mustard).
- **Pollination:** transfer of pollen to the stigma — **self** (same flower) or **cross** (another flower) by wind, water, insects and animals.
- A **pollen tube** grows from the pollen through the style to the ovule, carrying the male germ cell.
- **Fertilisation:** male germ cell fuses with the female germ cell (egg) in the ovule → **zygote** → **embryo**.
- After fertilisation: **ovule → seed** (with embryo and stored food); **ovary → fruit**; petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma usually shrivel and fall.
- **Germination:** the seed grows into a seedling (plumule → shoot, radicle → root) under suitable conditions.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — trace
steps.body: Pollen on anther → carried to stigma (pollination) → pollen tube through style → male gamete reaches ovule → fertilisation → zygote → embryo inside seed; ovary becomes fruit.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — germination activity
steps.body: Soak some gram (chana) seeds overnight, keep them in a damp cloth for a day, then split one: you can see the **plumule** (future shoot), **radicle** (future root) and **cotyledons** (stored food).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the ovary becomes the seed (the ovule becomes the seed; the ovary becomes the fruit).
- Saying pollination and fertilisation are the same.
- Calling papaya flowers bisexual.

activity.prompt: Order the events from pollination to fruit.
items: Pollen tube grows through the style
Male germ cell reaches the ovule
Ovule develops into a seed and ovary into a fruit

quiz.q: After fertilisation, the ovary develops into the
quiz.why: After fertilisation the ovary develops into the fruit and the ovules become seeds.

quiz.q: A unisexual flower:
quiz.why: Papaya has separate male and female flowers, so it is unisexual. Mustard, rose and Hibiscus flowers have both male and female parts.

quiz.q: Transfer of pollen to the stigma is
quiz.why: Transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma is pollination. Fertilisation is the fusion of gametes.

quiz.q: The part that develops into the future shoot:
quiz.why: The plumule develops into the shoot of the seedling, and the radicle into the root.

quiz.q: Germ cells contain
options: the same DNA amount as body cells
half the DNA of body cells
quiz.why: Germ cells have half the DNA of body cells. At fertilisation the full amount is restored.

quiz.q: The male part of a flower is the
quiz.why: The stamen (anther and filament) is the male part of a flower. The pistil is the female part.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (How do Organisms Reproduce?)

lessons.title: Reproduction in human beings

scenes.text: At 13, Arjun's voice is cracking and Riya has started her periods. Both feel shy asking questions.
Their biology teacher explains: these are normal changes of puberty, controlled by hormones.
Knowing the facts calmly and respectfully helps everyone look after their health.

steps.title: Puberty
steps.body:
Around ages 10–14 (it varies), the body prepares for reproductive maturity.

- **Both:** thicker hair in armpits and genital area, oily skin and pimples, growth spurt, new emotions and interest.
- **Boys:** facial hair, voice cracking/deepening, enlargement of the penis; occasional erection and night-time release of semen (nightfall) are normal.
- **Girls:** breast development, start of **menstruation** (periods).

These changes are controlled by **testosterone** (boys) and **oestrogen** (girls). Talk to a parent, teacher or doctor about any worries.

steps.title: Male reproductive system
steps.body:
- **Testes** make **sperms** and the hormone **testosterone**. They lie in the **scrotum**, outside the abdominal cavity, because sperm formation needs a temperature slightly **lower** than body temperature.
- **Vas deferens** carries sperms; it unites with a tube from the urinary bladder, so the **urethra** is a common passage for sperms and urine.
- **Seminal vesicles** and the **prostate gland** add secretions that make transport easier and provide nutrition. Sperms + secretions = **semen**.

steps.title: Female reproductive system
steps.body:
- Two **ovaries** make **eggs (ova)** and hormones (oestrogen). At birth a girl's ovaries already contain thousands of immature eggs; from puberty, usually **one egg** matures each month.
- The egg travels through the **oviduct (fallopian tube)**; **fertilisation** with a sperm, if it happens, takes place there.
- The **uterus** (bag-like, muscular) opens into the **vagina** through the **cervix**.
- The fertilised egg (zygote) implants in the thick uterine lining and grows into an embryo. The **placenta** (a disc-shaped tissue with villi) supplies glucose and oxygen from the mother's blood and removes wastes. Development takes about **nine months**; birth happens by rhythmic contraction of uterine muscles.
- If the egg is **not fertilised**, the thickened lining breaks down and is shed through the vagina as blood and mucus — **menstruation**, roughly every month, lasting about 2–8 days.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — why is the scrotum outside?
steps.body: Sperm formation needs a temperature lower than normal body temperature; the scrotum's position keeps the testes slightly cooler.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — role of the placenta
steps.body: The placenta provides a large surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from mother to embryo and for wastes to pass from embryo to the mother's blood, without mixing the two bloodstreams.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fertilisation occurs in the uterus (it occurs in the oviduct).
- Thinking periods are dirty or a sickness — menstruation is a normal body process.
- Believing myths about nightfall causing weakness — it is normal and harmless.

activity.prompt: Questions teens often hesitate to ask (answered factually)

items.q: Is it normal for puberty to start earlier or later than friends?
items.a: Yes. Puberty commonly begins between about 8–13 in girls and 9–14 in boys. If there are no signs by about 14 (girls) or 15 (boys), a doctor can check.
No. It is a normal release of semen during sleep in many boys and does not cause weakness.

items.q: How should periods be managed hygienically?
items.a: Use clean sanitary pads, cloth pads washed and dried in sunlight, tampons or menstrual cups; change regularly and wash hands. Mild cramps are common; very heavy bleeding or severe pain needs a doctor.
A parent, a trusted teacher, school counsellor or doctor. For help in India: Childline 1098, emergency 112, Tele-MANAS 14416 for feelings and stress.

quiz.q: Sperms are produced in the
quiz.why: Sperms are produced in the testes, the male gonads.

quiz.q: Fertilisation in humans usually occurs in the
quiz.why: Fertilisation in humans usually occurs in the oviduct (fallopian tube), where the egg meets sperm.

quiz.q: The placenta helps the embryo by
options: supplying nutrients and oxygen and removing wastes
quiz.why: The placenta lets the embryo get nutrients and oxygen from the mother's blood and pass wastes back to it.

quiz.q: Menstruation happens when
quiz.why: If the egg is not fertilised, the thickened uterine lining is shed with blood, which is menstruation. It is a normal part of the cycle.

quiz.q: Testes lie in the scrotum because
options: sperm formation needs a lower temperature
quiz.why: The testes lie in the scrotum outside the body because sperm formation needs a slightly lower temperature than body temperature.

quiz.q: A common passage for urine and sperms in males:
quiz.why: In males the urethra is the common passage for urine and sperms.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (How do Organisms Reproduce?)

lessons.title: Reproductive health

scenes.text: Kabir's friends share wrong 'facts' about sex on social media.
A school health talk gives accurate information about infections, contraception and the law.
Reliable knowledge protects health — your own and others'.

steps.title: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)
steps.body:
Infections passed through sexual contact:

- **Bacterial:** gonorrhoea, syphilis (curable with timely treatment).
- **Viral:** warts, **HIV-AIDS** (HIV can also spread through infected blood, shared needles and from mother to child).

Using a **condom** reduces the risk of transmission. Anyone with symptoms or concerns should see a doctor; testing and treatment are confidential.

steps.title: Contraception (preventing pregnancy)
steps.body:
- **Barrier methods:** condoms (also reduce STI risk).
- **Hormonal:** oral pills that change hormonal balance so eggs are not released (may have side effects; used under medical advice).
- **Intrauterine devices:** the loop or **copper-T** placed in the uterus by a doctor (may cause side effects).
- **Surgical:** **vasectomy** (vas deferens blocked in males) and **tubectomy** (fallopian tubes blocked in females). These are long-term and need a doctor.

The decision on family size and spacing is a personal and family decision taken with medical guidance.

steps.title: The law and society in India
steps.body:
- **Prenatal sex determination is illegal** in India; selecting the sex of a baby and **female foeticide** are crimes. A healthy sex ratio is vital for society.
- Under the **POCSO Act**, anyone below **18** is a child; children cannot legally consent to sexual activity, and adults who exploit them commit a serious offence.
- Help: Childline **1098**, emergency **112**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — classify
steps.body: Condom → barrier (also protects against STIs). Copper-T → intrauterine device. Oral pill → hormonal. Vasectomy → surgical (male).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing pills protect against STIs (they do not; condoms reduce risk).
- Thinking HIV spreads by hugging, sharing food or mosquito bites (it does not).
- Thinking sex determination tests are allowed 'just to know' — they are illegal.

activity.prompt: Classify each contraceptive method.

quiz.q: A viral STI:
quiz.why: HIV-AIDS is caused by a virus. Syphilis and gonorrhoea are bacterial, and tuberculosis is not an STI.

quiz.q: Which method also reduces the risk of STIs?
quiz.why: A condom is a barrier method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.

quiz.q: Vasectomy involves blocking the
quiz.why: In vasectomy the vas deferens is blocked so sperms cannot be carried out.

quiz.q: Prenatal sex determination in India is
quiz.why: Prenatal sex determination is illegal in India, to prevent female foeticide.

quiz.q: HIV does NOT spread by
quiz.why: HIV does not spread by sharing food or hugging. It spreads through infected blood, shared needles and from mother to child.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (How do Organisms Reproduce?)

questions.q: Binary fission occurs in
questions.why: Amoeba reproduces by binary fission, splitting into two daughter cells.

questions.q: The ovule after fertilisation becomes the
questions.why: After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

questions.q: The male germ cell in humans:
questions.why: The sperm is the male germ cell (gamete) in humans.

questions.q: Yeast reproduces asexually by
questions.why: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding, in which a small outgrowth forms on the parent cell and separates.

questions.q: Which plant is propagated vegetatively because it does not form viable seeds?
questions.why: Banana does not form viable seeds, so it is propagated vegetatively, for example from suckers. Orange can also be propagated this way.

questions.q: The female reproductive organ of a flower:
questions.why: The pistil (carpel) is the female part of a flower, made of stigma, style and ovary. The stamen is the male part.

questions.q: Assertion: Variation is more in sexually reproducing organisms. Reason: DNA from two parents combines in the offspring.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. In sexual reproduction DNA from two parents combines, giving new combinations and so more variation.

questions.q: Rhizopus spores are protected by
questions.why: Rhizopus spores are covered by thick walls that protect them until they reach moist conditions and can grow.

questions.q: Surgical method of contraception in females:
questions.why: Tubectomy, in which the fallopian tubes are blocked, is a surgical contraceptive method in females. Vasectomy is the male method.

questions.q: Case: A gardener wants many mango trees exactly like his best tree, bearing fruit quickly. He should use
questions.why: Grafting is vegetative propagation, so the new trees are identical to the best tree and often bear fruit sooner than trees grown from seed.

questions.q: Case continued: an advantage of this method over growing from seed is
options: the new plant keeps the parent's desirable traits
questions.why: Vegetative propagation gives genetically identical plants, so the new plant keeps the parent's desirable traits. Seeds give more variation.

questions.q: Why is DNA copying essential for reproduction?
options: Each new cell or organism needs a copy of the blueprint for body design
questions.why: DNA carries the blueprint for the body design. It is copied so that each new cell or organism gets the same instructions.

questions.q: Which is correctly matched?
questions.why: The prostate gland adds its secretions to the semen. The ovary makes eggs, fertilisation occurs in the oviduct, the uterus holds the embryo and the testis makes sperms.

questions.q: If the uterine lining thickens but no fertilisation occurs, then
options: the lining is shed as menstruation
questions.why: If there is no fertilisation, the thickened uterine lining is not needed and is shed as menstruation. It is a normal monthly cycle.

questions.q: Regeneration differs from fragmentation because
options: regeneration uses specialised cells to re-form organs from pieces
questions.why: Regeneration uses specialised cells that grow and re-form lost organs from pieces, as in Planaria and Hydra. Fragmentation just breaks the body into pieces that grow.

questions.q: Why does the zygote get the normal amount of DNA?
options: Zygote doubles its DNA after formation always
Each gamete carries half, and fusion restores the full set
questions.why: Each gamete carries half the DNA of a body cell. When they fuse at fertilisation, the full set is restored in the zygote.

questions.q: Which statement about HIV-AIDS is correct?
options: It is a viral infection that can spread through unprotected sexual contact and infected blood
It is caused by bacteria and cured by antibiotics
questions.why: HIV-AIDS is a viral infection, so antibiotics do not cure it. It spreads through unprotected sexual contact, infected blood and from mother to child, but not through utensils or mosquito bites.

questions.q: A pea plant flower is self-pollinated; a papaya needs cross-pollination. The reason is that
questions.why: Papaya has separate male and female flowers (unisexual), so pollen must be carried from one flower to another, which means cross-pollination. Pea flowers have both parts.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Heredity
courses.summary: How variations accumulate over generations, Mendel's pea-plant experiments with monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, how genes control traits, and how sex is determined in humans and other animals.
outcomes: Learners can explain how variations accumulate during reproduction
Learners can work out monohybrid crosses with Punnett squares and ratios
Learners can explain dominant and recessive traits and independent inheritance using a dihybrid cross
Learners can explain how genes control traits through proteins
Learners can explain sex determination in humans

scenes.text: Ananya has her grandfather's dimples but her mother's curly hair.
Her brother has neither — yet everyone looks like family.
Traits pass from parents to offspring with small variations each generation. That is heredity.

steps.title: Accumulation of variation
steps.body:
**Heredity** is the transmission of traits from parents to offspring. Inherited traits make offspring similar to parents, but not identical.

- In **asexual** reproduction, variation is small (only from minor DNA-copying errors).
- In **sexual** reproduction, variation is greater because DNA from two parents combines.
- Variations accumulate over generations. Some help survival in a particular environment; nature selects those (e.g. heat-resistant bacteria surviving a heat wave).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — interpret
steps.body: If a trait A exists in 10% of an asexually reproducing population and B in 60%, which arose earlier? **B** is likely older — it has had more time to spread through generations (assuming neither gives a special advantage).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — earlobes
steps.body: Free and attached earlobes are a visible human variation; surveys of a class show both types, and they run in families — an example of an inherited trait.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying offspring of sexual reproduction are identical to parents.
- Thinking all variations are useful.
- Confusing inherited traits with acquired ones (a scar or a learnt skill is not inherited).

activity.prompt: Inherited or acquired?

quiz.q: Variation is greater in
quiz.why: Sexual reproduction mixes DNA of two parents, so variation is greater than in asexual reproduction, where offspring are almost identical copies.

quiz.q: Transmission of traits from parents to offspring:
quiz.why: Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring through DNA. Variation is the differences among individuals.

quiz.q: An acquired trait:
quiz.why: A learnt language is an acquired trait, since it is not coded in DNA. Skin colour, eye colour and blood group are inherited.

quiz.q: In an asexual population, a trait found in more individuals likely arose
quiz.why: In an asexual population, a trait found in more individuals has had more generations to spread, so it likely arose earlier.

quiz.q: Variations that help survival are
quiz.why: Variations that help an organism survive are favoured by the environment, so they become more common. This is natural selection.

scenes.text: In the 1800s, Gregor Johann Mendel studied pea plants in a monastery garden.
He crossed tall plants with dwarf plants and counted the offspring carefully, generation after generation.
His counts revealed rules of inheritance that still hold today.

steps.title: The experiment
steps.body:
Mendel chose **contrasting traits** in garden peas: tall/short, round/wrinkled seeds, yellow/green seeds, violet/white flowers, etc.

- **Parent (P):** pure tall (TT) × pure dwarf (tt).
- **F1:** all **tall** (Tt) — no medium-height plants. The tall trait is **dominant**; dwarf is **recessive** (hidden).
- **F2 (F1 self-pollinated, Tt × Tt):** TT, Tt, Tt, tt → **3 tall : 1 dwarf** (phenotype); **1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt** (genotype).

So each trait is controlled by **two copies** of a factor (now called **genes**), one from each parent. A single copy of T is enough to make the plant tall.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — Punnett square for Tt × Tt
steps.body:
Gametes from each parent: T and t.

- T × T → TT (tall)
- T × t → Tt (tall)
- t × T → Tt (tall)
- t × t → tt (dwarf)

**Phenotype ratio 3 : 1; genotype ratio 1 : 2 : 1.**

steps.title: Solved example 2 — test the parent
steps.body: A tall plant crossed with a dwarf plant gives half tall and half dwarf offspring. The tall parent must be **Tt** (Tt × tt → 1 Tt : 1 tt). If it were TT, all offspring would be tall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that F1 plants are medium height (no blending).
- Mixing up phenotype (appearance) with genotype (gene combination).
- Thinking recessive traits disappear forever (they reappear in F2).

activity.prompt: Complete the F2 results of a monohybrid cross (Tt × Tt).
activity.text: Phenotype ratio tall : dwarf = ___ : 1. Fraction of plants that are pure tall (TT) = ___ (write as a fraction).

quiz.q: F1 of TT × tt is
quiz.why: T is dominant, so crossing TT with tt gives all Tt offspring, which are all tall.

quiz.q: F2 phenotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross:
quiz.why: In the F2 generation of a monohybrid cross the phenotypic ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

quiz.q: F2 genotypic ratio:
quiz.why: The F2 genotypes are TT, Tt and tt in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1.

quiz.q: The trait expressed in F1 is
quiz.why: The trait that shows up in F1 is the dominant trait. The other trait is recessive.

quiz.q: A cross of Tt × tt gives tall : dwarf =
quiz.why: Tt × tt gives half Tt (tall) and half tt (dwarf), a ratio of 1 : 1.

quiz.q: Mendel worked with
quiz.why: Mendel did his experiments on garden peas (Pisum sativum).

lessons.title: Dihybrid cross and how traits are expressed

scenes.text: Mendel next crossed plants with round, yellow seeds and plants with wrinkled, green seeds.
F1 were all round and yellow — but F2 showed new mixes like round green and wrinkled yellow.
Traits are inherited independently. And genes work by making proteins.

steps.title: Dihybrid cross
steps.body:
**P:** RRYY (round, yellow) × rryy (wrinkled, green). **F1:** all **RrYy** — round and yellow (both dominant).

**F2** (RrYy × RrYy) gives four kinds in the ratio **9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green**.

New combinations (round green, wrinkled yellow) appear, so the seed-shape and seed-colour traits are **inherited independently** of each other.

steps.title: How do genes control traits?
steps.body:
- A **gene** is a section of DNA that provides information for **one protein**.
- Example: plant height depends on a growth hormone; the amount of hormone depends on how efficiently an **enzyme** (a protein) makes it. An efficient enzyme (from the 'tall' gene) → lots of hormone → tall plant; a less efficient enzyme → less hormone → short plant.
- Genes are located on **chromosomes**. Each body cell has **two copies** of each chromosome, one from each parent. **Germ cells** have only **one** set, so fusion restores two copies in the offspring.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — read the F2 ratio
steps.body: Out of 1600 F2 seeds, expected: 900 round yellow, 300 round green, 300 wrinkled yellow, 100 wrinkled green (9 : 3 : 3 : 1).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — single-trait ratio inside a dihybrid
steps.body: In the F2 above, round : wrinkled = (9 + 3) : (3 + 1) = 12 : 4 = **3 : 1** — each trait alone still follows the monohybrid ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 as a genotype ratio (it is a phenotype ratio).
- Saying germ cells have two sets of chromosomes.
- Thinking one gene makes many unrelated traits directly (a gene codes for a protein).

activity.prompt: Match the F2 class of a dihybrid cross with its expected share out of 16.

quiz.q: F1 of RRYY × rryy is
quiz.why: R and Y are dominant over r and y, so RRYY × rryy gives all RrYy, which are round and yellow.

quiz.q: F2 phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross:
quiz.why: The F2 phenotypic ratio in a dihybrid cross is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

quiz.q: Appearance of round green seeds in F2 shows
quiz.why: Round green seeds are a new combination that appears in F2. This shows that the two traits are inherited independently.

quiz.q: A gene provides information for making
quiz.why: A gene is a section of DNA that provides the information for making a particular protein.

quiz.q: Germ cells carry
quiz.why: Germ cells carry one set of chromosomes, which is half of the number in body cells.

quiz.q: In 1600 F2 seeds, wrinkled green expected:
quiz.why: Wrinkled green seeds are 1/16 of the F2 in a dihybrid cross, so 1/16 × 1600 = 100.

scenes.text: When a baby girl is born, a relative wrongly blames the mother for 'not having a boy'.
The biology teacher explains: the sex of a human baby is decided by the father's sperm, by chance.
Science replaces blame with facts — and a girl child is equally welcome.

steps.title: How sex is determined
steps.body:
- In some animals, it depends on **environment**: in some reptiles the **temperature** at which eggs are incubated decides the sex. Some snails can **change sex**.
- In **humans**, sex is genetically determined. Of 23 pairs of chromosomes, **22 pairs** are autosomes; one pair is the **sex chromosomes**.
- Women have **XX**; men have **XY** (Y is shorter).
- Every egg carries an **X**. Half of the sperms carry **X** and half carry **Y**.
- **X sperm + egg → XX → girl; Y sperm + egg → XY → boy.** So the chance is about **50 : 50**, and it is the **sperm** that determines the sex.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — Punnett square
steps.body: Mother's gametes: X, X. Father's gametes: X, Y. Offspring: XX, XX, XY, XY → **1 girl : 1 boy** (probability ½ each).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — expose a myth
steps.body: 'A woman is responsible for the sex of her child' — false. The mother always gives X; the father gives X or Y.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the mother decides the sex.
- Writing that men have XX.
- Saying humans have 23 chromosomes in total (they have 23 pairs = 46).

statements.s: In humans, the father's sperm determines the sex of the child.
Women have XY chromosomes.
In some reptiles, incubation temperature decides the sex.
Human body cells have 23 chromosomes.
The chance of a baby being a girl is about 50%.

quiz.q: Sex chromosomes of a human male:
quiz.why: A human male has one X and one Y chromosome, so XY.

quiz.q: Number of autosome pairs in humans:
quiz.why: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes, making 23 pairs in all.

quiz.q: An egg always carries
quiz.why: A female is XX, so every egg carries an X chromosome.

quiz.q: Probability that a child is a boy:
quiz.why: Half of the sperms carry X and half carry Y, so the probability that a child is a boy is 1/2.

quiz.q: In some snails, sex
quiz.why: In some animals, such as certain snails, sex can change during life instead of being fixed by chromosomes.

questions.q: The units of heredity are
questions.why: The units of heredity are genes, which are sections of DNA.

questions.q: In Mendel's cross, tall is
questions.why: All the F1 plants are tall, so tall is dominant over dwarf.

questions.q: Sex chromosomes of a human female:
questions.why: A human female has two X chromosomes, so XX.

questions.q: Number of chromosomes in a human body cell:
questions.why: A human body cell has 23 pairs of chromosomes, which is 46 in all.

questions.q: The F2 ratio 3 : 1 refers to
questions.why: The 3 : 1 ratio describes how the plants look (tall and dwarf), so it is a phenotypic ratio.

questions.q: Which is an inherited trait?
questions.why: Blood group is inherited through genes. A cut, a haircut and a spoken language are not inherited.

questions.q: Assertion: F1 plants of TT × tt are all tall. Reason: one copy of T is enough to express tallness.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. T is dominant, so one copy of T is enough to make the plant tall, and all F1 plants (Tt) are tall.

questions.q: A cross between Tt and Tt produces dwarf plants in the proportion
questions.why: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Only tt is dwarf, so the proportion is 1/4.

questions.q: Genotype of a dwarf pea plant:
questions.why: Dwarf is the recessive trait, so it shows only when both copies are t. Its genotype is tt.

questions.q: Case: A couple has three daughters. A neighbour says the fourth child will surely be a son. The probability of a son is
questions.why: Each birth is an independent event. The father's sperm carries X or Y with equal chance, so the chance of a son is 1/2 even after three daughters.

questions.q: Case continued: who determines the sex of the child?
questions.why: The egg always carries X, but a sperm carries X or Y. So the father's sperm decides the sex of the child.

questions.q: In a dihybrid F2 of 320 seeds, round green seeds expected:
questions.why: Round green seeds are 3/16 of the F2. 3/16 × 320 = 60.

questions.q: Mendel's dihybrid results showed new combinations. This proves
questions.why: New combinations of traits in the dihybrid F2 show that traits are inherited independently of each other.

questions.q: How does a gene for tallness make a plant tall?
options: It codes for an efficient enzyme that makes more growth hormone
questions.why: A gene for tallness codes for an efficient enzyme that makes more growth hormone, and this makes the plant tall. A gene works through the protein it makes.

questions.q: A tall plant crossed with a dwarf gives 52 tall and 48 dwarf offspring. The tall parent's genotype is
questions.why: About 1 : 1 tall and dwarf offspring means the cross is Tt × tt. So the tall parent is Tt.

questions.q: If a trait is recessive, which statement is true?
options: It appears only when both copies are recessive
questions.why: A recessive trait appears only when both copies of the gene are recessive (for example tt). One dominant copy hides it.

lessons.title: Reflection and spherical mirrors

scenes.text: Isha looks at herself in a shiny steel spoon. The inner side shows her upside down; the back side shows her small and upright.
The spoon's two sides behave like concave and convex mirrors.
Both follow the same two laws of reflection.

steps.title: Laws of reflection
steps.body:
1. The **angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection**.
2. The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected ray lie in the **same plane**.

These apply to all reflecting surfaces, including curved ones. A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, laterally inverted.

steps.title: Spherical mirror terms
steps.body:
- **Concave** mirror: reflecting surface curved inwards (converging). **Convex**: curved outwards (diverging).
- **Pole (P):** centre of the reflecting surface.
- **Centre of curvature (C):** centre of the sphere the mirror is part of (in front of a concave mirror, behind a convex one).
- **Radius of curvature (R):** distance PC.
- **Principal axis:** line through P and C.
- **Principal focus (F):** point where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflection.
- **Focal length f = PF, and R = 2f** (for small apertures).
- **Aperture:** the diameter of the reflecting surface.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — R and f
steps.body: A concave mirror has R = 32 cm. Its focal length is **16 cm**. A convex mirror with f = 15 cm has R = **30 cm**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — sunlight test
steps.body: Hold a concave mirror facing the Sun and focus the light on a sheet of paper; the paper may start to burn at the bright spot — that spot is the focus. (Do not look at the Sun or its reflection directly.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the centre of curvature is a point on the mirror (that is the pole).
- Writing f = 2R.
- Forgetting that F and C of a convex mirror lie behind it.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its description.
pairs: Centre of the sphere it is part of
Point where parallel rays meet after reflection (concave)
Relation between radius and focal length

quiz.q: Angle of incidence equals
quiz.why: By the first law of reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

quiz.q: If R = 20 cm, f =
quiz.why: For a spherical mirror, f = R/2 = 20/2 = 10 cm.

quiz.q: A concave mirror is
quiz.why: A concave mirror is a converging mirror, because parallel rays meet at its focus after reflection.

quiz.q: The image in a plane mirror is
quiz.why: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image the same size as the object.

quiz.q: The line through the pole and centre of curvature is the
quiz.why: The straight line through the pole and the centre of curvature is the principal axis.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Light – Reflection and Refraction)

lessons.title: Images formed by spherical mirrors

story.title: Torch, shaving mirror and rear-view mirror

scenes.text: A torch uses a concave mirror to throw a strong parallel beam.
A shaving mirror makes the face look bigger.
A car's rear-view mirror is convex — it shows a wide view, always upright.

steps.title: Rays for diagrams
steps.body:
1. A ray parallel to the axis passes through F (concave) or appears to come from F (convex) after reflection.
2. A ray through F (or directed towards F) becomes parallel to the axis.
3. A ray through C (or directed towards C) returns along the same path.
4. A ray hitting the pole obliquely reflects at an equal angle on the other side of the axis.

steps.title: Concave mirror image table
steps.body:
- Object at **infinity** → image at **F**; highly diminished, real, inverted.
- **Beyond C** → between **F and C**; diminished, real, inverted.
- **At C** → **at C**; same size, real, inverted.
- **Between C and F** → **beyond C**; enlarged, real, inverted.
- **At F** → **at infinity**; highly enlarged, real, inverted.
- **Between P and F** → **behind the mirror**; enlarged, **virtual, erect**.

**Convex mirror:** always **between P and F behind the mirror**, diminished, virtual, erect (object anywhere).

steps.title: Uses
steps.body:
- **Concave:** torches, searchlights and vehicle headlights (bulb at F gives a parallel beam); shaving and make-up mirrors (enlarged erect image when face is within F); dentists' mirrors; solar furnaces (concentrate sunlight).
- **Convex:** rear-view (wing) mirrors — always erect, diminished image and a **wider field of view**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — choose position
steps.body: To get a real image of the same size with a concave mirror of f = 15 cm, place the object at C, i.e. **30 cm** from the mirror.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a convex mirror can form a real image of a real object.
- Saying a concave mirror always gives an inverted image (not when the object is between P and F).
- Saying rear-view mirrors are concave.

activity.prompt: For a concave mirror, is the image real or virtual?

quiz.q: Image formed by a convex mirror is always
quiz.why: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, wherever the object is placed.

quiz.q: For an enlarged erect image from a concave mirror, the object must be
quiz.why: A concave mirror gives an enlarged, erect, virtual image when the object is between the pole P and the focus F. A shaving mirror works this way.

quiz.q: Headlights use concave mirrors with the bulb at
quiz.why: The bulb is at the focus of the concave reflector, so the reflected rays form a parallel beam.

quiz.q: Object at C of a concave mirror gives an image
quiz.why: With the object at C of a concave mirror, the image forms at C, the same size and inverted.

quiz.q: Rear-view mirrors are convex because they
options: give an erect image with a wider field of view
quiz.why: Rear-view mirrors are convex because they give an erect image and a much wider field of view.

quiz.q: A ray through C after reflection
quiz.why: A ray through the centre of curvature meets the mirror at 90° and so retraces its path.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Light – Reflection and Refraction)

lessons.title: Mirror formula and magnification

scenes.text: Instead of drawing every diagram, physicists use one formula linking object distance, image distance and focal length.
A sign convention keeps track of which side each distance is on.
Signs of v and m then tell you whether the image is real or virtual, erect or inverted.

steps.title: New Cartesian sign convention
steps.body:
- The **pole** is the origin; the principal axis is the x-axis.
- The **object** is placed to the **left** of the mirror, so **u is negative**.
- Distances measured to the **right** (along incident light) are **positive**; to the left, **negative**.
- Heights **above** the axis are positive; **below** negative.

So: concave mirror **f negative**; convex mirror **f positive**.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
**Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f**

**Magnification: m = h′/h = −v/u**

- m negative → real, inverted; m positive → virtual, erect.
- |m| > 1 enlarged; |m| < 1 diminished.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — concave mirror
steps.body:
Object 4 cm tall at 25 cm from a concave mirror of f = 15 cm. u = −25, f = −15.

1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/15 + 1/25 = (−5 + 3)/75 = −2/75 → **v = −37.5 cm** (in front, real).

m = −v/u = −(−37.5)/(−25) = **−1.5**; h′ = −1.5 × 4 = **−6 cm** (inverted, enlarged).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — convex mirror
steps.body:
Object at 30 cm from a convex mirror of f = 20 cm. u = −30, f = +20.

1/v = 1/20 + 1/30 = 5/60 → **v = +12 cm** (behind mirror, virtual). m = −12/(−30) = **+0.4** (erect, diminished).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — find the object position
steps.body: A concave mirror (f = 10 cm) forms an image at 20 cm in front of it (v = −20). 1/u = 1/f − 1/v = −1/10 + 1/20 = −1/20 → **u = −20 cm**: object at C, image same size, inverted (m = −1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that u is always negative.
- Using + sign for the focal length of a concave mirror.
- Writing m = v/u for mirrors (the mirror formula needs the minus sign: m = −v/u).

activity.prompt: A concave mirror has f = 12 cm. An object is placed 18 cm in front. Find v (with sign, in cm).

quiz.q: Focal length of a concave mirror in the sign convention is
quiz.why: In the sign convention, the focus of a concave mirror lies in front of it, on the object side, so its focal length is negative.

quiz.q: Magnification for mirrors:
quiz.why: The magnification for mirrors is m = −v/u.

quiz.q: If m = −2, the image is
quiz.why: A negative m means the image is inverted and real. |m| = 2 means it is enlarged twice.

quiz.q: Convex mirror f = 20 cm, object at 30 cm: v =
quiz.why: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/20 + 1/30 = 5/60, so v = +12 cm. The image is virtual and behind the mirror.

quiz.q: Object distance u is always
quiz.why: The object is placed on the left of the mirror, which is the negative side, so u is always negative.

quiz.q: For a plane mirror, magnification is
quiz.why: A plane mirror forms an erect image of the same size, so m = +1.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Light – Reflection and Refraction)

lessons.title: Refraction and refractive index

scenes.text: A pencil dipped in a glass of water looks broken at the surface.
A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
Light changes speed and direction when it passes from one medium into another — refraction.

steps.title: Laws of refraction
steps.body:
1. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the **same plane**.
2. **Snell's law:** for a given pair of media and a given colour of light, **sin i / sin r = constant** = refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.

Light going from a **rarer to a denser** medium (air → glass) slows down and bends **towards** the normal; from denser to rarer it bends **away** from the normal. A ray along the normal goes straight.

steps.title: Refractive index
steps.body:
**n₂₁ = v₁/v₂** (speed in medium 1 ÷ speed in medium 2).

**Absolute refractive index:** n = c/v, where c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s (speed of light in vacuum).

Some values: air 1.0003, water 1.33, kerosene 1.44, crown glass 1.52, diamond 2.42. Higher n = **optically denser** (light is slower). Optical density is not the same as mass density (kerosene is optically denser than water but floats on it).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — relative index
steps.body: n(water) = 1.33, n(glass) = 1.5. Refractive index of glass w.r.t. water = 1.5/1.33 ≈ **1.13**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — glass slab
steps.body: Light through a rectangular glass slab bends towards the normal entering and away from it leaving. The emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray but **laterally displaced**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying light bends away from the normal entering glass from air.
- Thinking optically denser means heavier.
- Writing n = v/c (it is c/v).

statements.s: Light slows down when it enters glass from air.
The emergent ray from a glass slab is parallel to the incident ray.
Kerosene is optically denser than water.
A ray along the normal bends at the surface.
Diamond has the lowest refractive index of common materials.

quiz.q: Speed of light in a medium of refractive index 1.5:
Light from air into glass bends
quiz.why: Light going from a rarer medium (air) to a denser medium (glass) bends towards the normal.

quiz.q: Snell's law states that
options: sin i / sin r is constant
quiz.why: Snell's law states that sin i/sin r is a constant for a given pair of media.

quiz.q: Which has the highest refractive index?
quiz.why: Diamond has a refractive index of about 2.42, which is the highest of these.

quiz.q: A pool appears shallower because of
quiz.why: A pool looks shallower because light bends (refracts) as it leaves the water.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Light – Reflection and Refraction)

lessons.title: Spherical lenses and their images

scenes.text: Kabir uses a magnifying glass to read tiny print — the letters look larger and upright.
Held far from paper in sunlight, the same lens makes a tiny bright spot.
His father's spectacles for distant vision, however, make things look smaller. Convex and concave lenses differ.

steps.title: Lens terms
steps.body:
- **Convex lens:** thicker at the middle — **converging**. **Concave lens:** thinner at the middle — **diverging**.
- **Optical centre (O):** centre of the lens; a ray through it goes undeviated.
- Two centres of curvature, so two foci: **F₁** and **F₂**; focal length f = OF. Also 2F₁ and 2F₂ at twice the focal length.

**Rays:** parallel to axis → through F₂ (convex) or appears from F₁ (concave); through F₁ → emerges parallel (convex), towards F₂ → parallel (concave); through O → undeviated.

steps.title: Convex lens image table
steps.body:
- Object at **infinity** → at **F₂**; highly diminished, real, inverted.
- **Beyond 2F₁** → **between F₂ and 2F₂**; diminished, real, inverted.
- **At 2F₁** → **at 2F₂**; same size, real, inverted.
- **Between F₁ and 2F₁** → **beyond 2F₂**; enlarged, real, inverted.
- **At F₁** → **at infinity**; highly enlarged.
- **Between F₁ and O** → **same side as object**; enlarged, **virtual, erect** (magnifying glass).

**Concave lens:** always **between F₁ and O**, diminished, virtual, erect (at F₁ when the object is at infinity).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — choose the lens
steps.body: To read small print with an enlarged, erect image: a **convex lens** with the print **within its focal length**. To form a real image on a screen of the same size: object at **2F₁** of a convex lens.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — concave lens image
steps.body: Object anywhere in front of a concave lens → virtual, erect, diminished image between F₁ and O. A concave lens can **never** form a real image of a real object.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up mirrors and lenses: a convex **mirror** diverges but a convex **lens** converges.
- Saying the image of a magnifying glass is real.
- Forgetting a ray through the optical centre goes straight.

activity.prompt: Convex lens: match object position with image position.

quiz.q: A convex lens is
quiz.why: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges parallel rays.

quiz.q: A ray through the optical centre
quiz.why: A ray passing through the optical centre of a thin lens goes straight without deviation.

quiz.q: Image by a concave lens is always
quiz.why: A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image for a real object.

quiz.q: A magnifying glass uses a convex lens with the object
quiz.why: A magnifying glass is a convex lens with the object between the focus F₁ and the optical centre O. It then forms a virtual, erect, enlarged image.

quiz.q: For a same-size real image with a convex lens, object at
quiz.why: With the object at 2F₁, a convex lens forms a real, inverted image at 2F₂ of the same size.

quiz.q: Which can form a real image?
quiz.why: A convex lens can form a real image when the object is beyond F. Plane and convex mirrors and concave lenses never form real images for real objects.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Light – Reflection and Refraction)

lessons.title: Lens formula, magnification and power

scenes.text: Riya's spectacle prescription says −2.0 D. What does the D mean?
D is dioptre, the unit of power of a lens — the reciprocal of focal length in metres.
With the lens formula and power, you can solve any lens numerical.

steps.title: Formulas (same sign convention)
steps.body:
**Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f**

**Magnification: m = h′/h = v/u** (no minus sign for lenses)

**Power: P = 1/f** (f in **metres**); unit **dioptre (D)**. 1 D = power of a lens of focal length 1 m.
- Convex lens: f and P **positive**; concave: **negative**.
- Lenses in contact: **P = P₁ + P₂ + …**

steps.title: Solved example 1 — convex lens
steps.body:
Object 2 cm tall at 15 cm from a convex lens of f = 10 cm. u = −15, f = +10.

1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 → **v = +30 cm** (other side, real).

m = v/u = 30/(−15) = **−2**; h′ = **−4 cm** (inverted, enlarged).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — concave lens
steps.body:
Object at 10 cm from a concave lens of f = 15 cm. u = −10, f = −15.

1/v = −1/15 − 1/10 = −5/30 → **v = −6 cm** (same side, virtual). m = −6/(−10) = **+0.6** (erect, diminished).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — power
steps.body: Concave lens f = 2 m → P = −0.5 D. Convex lens f = 50 cm = 0.5 m → P = **+2 D**. Two lenses of +2.0 D and −0.5 D in contact → P = **+1.5 D**, f = 1/1.5 ≈ 0.67 m (converging).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using f in centimetres in P = 1/f (convert to metres, or use P = 100/f with f in cm).
- Using the mirror formula (1/v + 1/u) for lenses.
- Adding focal lengths instead of powers for lenses in contact.

activity.prompt: A convex lens has f = 20 cm. Find its power in dioptres.

quiz.q: Lens formula:
quiz.why: The lens formula is 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. For mirrors it is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.

quiz.q: Power of a concave lens of focal length 2 m:
quiz.why: Power P = 1/f. For a concave lens with f = −2 m, P = −0.5 D.

quiz.q: Magnification for lenses:
quiz.why: For lenses the magnification is m = v/u, without a minus sign.

quiz.q: Convex lens f = 10 cm, object at 15 cm: image distance
Net power of lenses +2.0 D and −0.5 D in contact:
quiz.why: The powers of lenses in contact add: +2.0 + (−0.5) = +1.5 D.

quiz.q: 1 dioptre is the power of a lens of focal length
quiz.why: One dioptre is the power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre.

questions.why: For a spherical mirror, the radius of curvature is twice the focal length: R = 2f.

questions.q: Mirror used as a rear-view mirror:
questions.why: A convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror because it gives an erect image and a wide field of view.

questions.q: SI unit of power of a lens:
questions.why: The SI unit of power of a lens is the dioptre (D).

questions.q: Refractive index of water is about
questions.why: The refractive index of water is about 1.33.

questions.q: A concave lens is also called a
questions.why: A concave lens spreads parallel rays, so it is a diverging lens.

questions.q: Image formed by a convex mirror is
questions.why: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.

questions.q: Assertion: A concave mirror is used in solar furnaces. Reason: it converges sunlight to its focus.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. A concave mirror converges sunlight to its focus, which concentrates heat in a solar furnace.

questions.q: If the magnification of a lens is +3, the image is
questions.why: A positive magnification greater than 1 means the image is erect (virtual) and enlarged.

questions.q: Speed of light in diamond (n = 2.42) is approximately
Case: A student focuses a distant tree on a screen with a convex lens; the screen is 20 cm from the lens. The focal length is
questions.why: The image of a distant object forms at the focus, so the screen distance, 20 cm, is the focal length.

questions.q: Case continued: the power of this lens is
questions.why: P = 1/f = 1/0.20 m = +5 D, positive for a convex lens.

questions.q: A concave mirror of f = 10 cm with object at 30 cm. Image distance:
questions.why: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/10 + 1/30 = −2/30, so v = −15 cm. The image is real and in front of the mirror.

questions.q: An object 5 cm tall is 20 cm from a convex lens of f = 10 cm. The image height is
questions.why: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/20 = 1/20, so v = 20 cm and m = v/u = −1. The image is 5 cm tall and inverted, so its height is −5 cm.

questions.q: A ray of light enters water from air at an angle. Compared with the incident ray, the refracted ray
questions.why: Going from air (rarer) to water (denser), the refracted ray bends towards the normal.

questions.q: A concave lens of f = 15 cm forms an image 10 cm from the lens. The object distance is
questions.why: With f = −15 and v = −10, 1/u = 1/v − 1/f = −1/10 + 1/15 = −1/30. So u = −30 cm, an object distance of 30 cm.

questions.q: A convex mirror used on a car has R = 3.00 m. A bus is 5.00 m behind. The image is formed at about
questions.why: f = R/2 = +1.5 m. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/1.5 + 1/5 = 13/15, so v ≈ +1.15 m, which is behind the mirror.

questions.q: Two lenses of power +3.5 D and −2.5 D are placed in contact. The combination is
questions.why: Net power = +3.5 + (−2.5) = +1 D. A positive power means converging, and f = 1/1 = 1 m.

lessons.title: The human eye

scenes.text: Zoya's camera has a lens, an adjustable opening and a sensor.
Her eye has the same plan: cornea and lens focus, iris controls the opening, retina senses the image.
But the eye can also change its focal length — something a fixed camera lens cannot do.

steps.title: Parts and functions
steps.body:
- **Cornea:** transparent bulge in front; **most of the refraction** of light happens here.
- **Iris:** dark muscular diaphragm that controls the size of the **pupil**.
- **Pupil:** opening that regulates the light entering the eye (small in bright light, large in dim light).
- **Crystalline (eye) lens:** fine-adjusts focus to form a **real, inverted** image on the retina.
- **Ciliary muscles:** change the curvature and thus focal length of the lens.
- **Retina:** light-sensitive screen with **rods** (dim light) and **cones** (colour); it sends electrical signals through the **optic nerve** to the brain, which interprets the image.

steps.title: Power of accommodation
steps.body:
The eye lens adjusts its focal length to see near and far objects:

- **Far objects:** ciliary muscles **relax**, lens becomes **thin**, focal length **increases**.
- **Near objects:** ciliary muscles **contract**, lens becomes **thick**, focal length **decreases**.

**Near point** (least distance of distinct vision) of a normal young adult ≈ **25 cm**; **far point** = **infinity**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — why we cannot see clearly closer than 25 cm
steps.body: The lens cannot become thicker (more converging) beyond a limit, so objects closer than about 25 cm cannot be focused on the retina; they look blurred.

steps.title: Cataract and eye donation
steps.body: In some older people the lens becomes milky and cloudy — **cataract** — causing partial or complete loss of vision; it can be treated by surgery. Eyes can be **donated after death**; the cornea can restore sight to people with corneal blindness. Eye banks need the eyes to be removed within a few hours of death.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the eye lens does most of the refraction (the cornea does).
- Saying the image on the retina is erect (it is inverted; the brain interprets it).
- Mixing up iris (controls size) and pupil (the opening).

activity.prompt: Match the part of the eye with its job.

quiz.q: The image formed on the retina is
quiz.why: The eye forms a real, inverted image on the retina. The brain interprets it as upright.

quiz.q: Near point of a normal eye:
quiz.why: The near point of a normal eye, the least distance of distinct vision, is 25 cm.

quiz.q: To see distant objects, ciliary muscles
quiz.why: To see distant objects the ciliary muscles relax, the lens becomes thin and its focal length increases.

quiz.q: Cells in the retina sensitive to colour:
quiz.why: Cones are sensitive to colour and bright light. Rods work in dim light.

quiz.q: Pupil size is controlled by the
quiz.why: The iris controls the size of the pupil, and so how much light enters the eye.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (The Human Eye and the Colourful World)

lessons.title: Defects of vision and their correction

scenes.text: Arjun sits at the back of class and cannot read the board, but reads his book perfectly.
His grandmother reads the newspaper only at arm's length.
Different defects need different lenses. Let us diagnose each one.

steps.title: Myopia (near-sightedness)
steps.body:
Near objects are clear; **far objects blurred**. The far point is nearer than infinity; the image of a distant object forms **in front of the retina**.

Causes: excessive curvature of the eye lens, or elongation of the eyeball.

Correction: **concave lens** of suitable power (negative).

steps.title: Hypermetropia (far-sightedness)
steps.body:
Far objects are clear; **near objects blurred**. The near point is farther than 25 cm; light from a near object focuses **behind the retina**.

Causes: focal length of the eye lens too long, or eyeball too short.

Correction: **convex lens** of suitable power (positive).

steps.title: Presbyopia
steps.body: With age, accommodation weakens (ciliary muscles weaken, lens less flexible); the near point recedes. Some people have both myopia and hypermetropia — they use **bifocal lenses** (upper concave part for distance, lower convex part for reading). Contact lenses and surgery are other options.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — myopia numerical
steps.body: A person's far point is 80 cm. A lens must form the image of a distant object (u = −∞) at 80 cm (v = −80 cm): 1/f = 1/v − 1/u = −1/80 → f = **−80 cm**, P = 100/(−80) = **−1.25 D** (concave).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a convex lens for myopia.
- Saying in hypermetropia the image forms in front of the retina.
- Forgetting to convert cm to m when finding power (P = 100/f with f in cm).

activity.prompt: Match the feature to the defect.

items.text: Image forms in front of the retina

lessons.title: Prism, dispersion and the rainbow

scenes.text: Sunlight through a glass prism on the window sill throws a band of colours on the wall.
Newton showed that white light is made of all these colours, and a second prism can join them back.
Raindrops do the same in the sky after a shower.

steps.title: Refraction through a prism
steps.body: A triangular glass **prism** has two refracting surfaces inclined at the **angle of the prism**. Light bends towards the base twice. The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray is the **angle of deviation**.

steps.title: Dispersion
steps.body:
Splitting of white light into its component colours is **dispersion**. The band of colours is the **spectrum**: **VIBGYOR** — Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.

Different colours bend by different amounts: **red bends the least, violet the most** (different colours travel at different speeds in glass).

**Newton** placed a second, inverted prism and got white light back — proving white light is a mixture of colours. Any light that gives a spectrum like sunlight is called white light.

steps.title: Rainbow
steps.body: A rainbow is a natural spectrum seen **after a rain shower**, in the sky **opposite to the Sun**. Tiny water droplets act like small prisms: light is **refracted and dispersed** on entering a droplet, **internally reflected** inside, and refracted again on leaving.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — explain
steps.body: Why does violet deviate more than red in a prism? Violet light slows down more in glass (glass has a higher refractive index for violet), so it bends more.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — when to see a rainbow
steps.body: In the late afternoon after rain, stand with your **back to the Sun** and look towards the sky in front of you (east) — the rainbow appears there. You can also make one with a water sprayer with the Sun behind you.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a prism 'adds' colours to light (they were already present).
- Saying red bends the most.
- Looking for a rainbow towards the Sun.

activity.prompt: Arrange the colours of the spectrum from the least deviated to the most deviated.

quiz.q: Splitting of white light into colours is
quiz.why: The splitting of white light into its colours is dispersion.

quiz.q: The colour that bends the least in a prism:
quiz.why: Red light has the longest wavelength and bends the least in a prism. Violet bends the most.

quiz.q: Newton's second inverted prism showed that
options: white light is made of colours
quiz.why: Newton's second inverted prism recombined the colours into white light, showing that white light is made of colours.

quiz.q: A rainbow forms due to
options: refraction, dispersion and internal reflection in droplets
quiz.why: A rainbow forms by refraction and dispersion of sunlight in raindrops, followed by internal reflection and a second refraction.

quiz.q: A rainbow is seen
quiz.why: A rainbow is seen opposite to the Sun, with the Sun behind the observer.

lessons.title: Atmospheric refraction and scattering

scenes.text: At sunset, Meera sees the Sun turn orange-red and look slightly flattened.
Later the stars twinkle, but the planets shine steadily.
Air bends and scatters light — creating these everyday wonders.

steps.title: Atmospheric refraction
steps.body:
Air layers of different temperature and density have different refractive indices, so starlight and sunlight bend as they pass through.

- **Twinkling of stars:** stars are distant point sources; changing atmospheric conditions keep shifting their apparent position and brightness → twinkling. Stars appear slightly **higher** than they really are near the horizon.
- **Planets do not twinkle:** they are much closer and act as extended sources (a collection of points); variations average out.
- **Advance sunrise and delayed sunset:** we see the Sun about **2 minutes before** actual sunrise and about **2 minutes after** actual sunset. The flattened look of the Sun at sunrise/sunset is also due to refraction.
- The wavering, flickering appearance of objects seen through hot air above a fire is also atmospheric refraction.

steps.title: Scattering of light
steps.body:
- **Tyndall effect:** a beam of light is visible when it passes through a colloid (smoke, mist, dust) because particles scatter light — e.g. sunlight entering a dense forest canopy or a dusty room.
- **Colour depends on particle size:** very fine particles scatter mainly **blue** (shorter wavelength); larger particles scatter all colours (so clouds look **white**).
- **Blue sky:** air molecules scatter blue much more than red. Above the atmosphere (for astronauts) the sky looks **dark** because there is little scattering.
- **Reddish Sun at sunrise and sunset:** light travels a **longer path** through air; most blue is scattered away, and mostly **red** reaches our eyes. At noon the path is short, so the Sun looks white.
- **Danger signals are red** because red is scattered least and can be seen from far away, even in fog.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — explain
steps.body: Why do stars twinkle but not planets? Stars are point sources whose light keeps bending by varying amounts; planets are extended sources so the overall brightness stays steady.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — sky colour
steps.body: If the Earth had no atmosphere, the sky would look **dark** even in daytime, because there would be nothing to scatter sunlight.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying stars twinkle because they switch on and off.
- Saying the sky is blue because it reflects the ocean.
- Saying the Sun looks red at sunset because it cools down.

statements.s: Planets twinkle as much as stars.
We see the Sun about 2 minutes before actual sunrise.
Clouds are white because large droplets scatter all colours.
Danger signals are red because red scatters the most.
To an astronaut in space, the sky appears dark.

quiz.q: Twinkling of stars is due to
quiz.why: Stars twinkle because of atmospheric refraction, as light passes through air layers of changing density.

quiz.q: The sky appears blue because
options: air molecules scatter blue light more
quiz.why: The sky is blue because air molecules scatter blue light more than red light.

quiz.q: The Sun looks reddish at sunrise because
options: light travels a longer path and blue is scattered away
quiz.why: At sunrise sunlight travels a longer path through the air, so most blue light is scattered away and red reaches us.

quiz.q: The Tyndall effect is
options: scattering of light by colloidal particles
quiz.why: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles, which makes the path of a light beam visible.

quiz.q: Advance sunrise is about
quiz.why: Because of atmospheric refraction, the Sun is seen about 2 minutes before it actually rises.

quiz.q: Why are danger signals red?
options: Red is scattered least and seen from far
quiz.why: Red light is scattered the least and has the longest wavelength, so danger signals in red can be seen from far away.

options: A second inverted prism recombines the spectrum into white light
questions.why: A second inverted prism recombines the spectrum into white light, which shows that white light is a mixture of colours.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Electricity
courses.summary: Electric charge and current, potential difference, Ohm's law, resistance and resistivity, series and parallel circuits, the heating effect of current and electric power and energy — with step-by-step numericals and household examples.
outcomes: Learners can define current, potential difference and resistance with SI units
Learners can state and verify Ohm's law
Learners can use R = ρl/A and explain factors affecting resistance
Learners can solve series and parallel circuit problems
Learners can apply H = I²Rt, P = VI and compute energy in kWh and its cost

scenes.text: Kavya's torch stays dark until she tightens the cap — then it glows.
The cap completes a closed path from the cell through the bulb and back.
Charge flows only in a closed path: an electric circuit.

steps.title: Current
steps.body:
**Electric current** is the rate of flow of charge: **I = Q/t**.

- SI unit of charge: **coulomb (C)**; of current: **ampere (A)**. 1 A = 1 C/s. Small currents: mA (10⁻³ A), μA (10⁻⁶ A).
- Charge of an electron = **1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C** (negative); 1 C ≈ **6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons**.
- In metal wires, **electrons** carry the charge. By convention, **current flows from positive to negative terminal**, opposite to electron flow.
- **Ammeter** measures current; it is connected **in series**.

steps.title: Circuit symbols
steps.body: Cell (long line +, short line −), battery (several cells), plug key or switch (open/closed), wire joint, wires crossing without joining, bulb, resistor (zig-zag), variable resistor/rheostat (zig-zag with arrow), ammeter (A in a circle), voltmeter (V in a circle).

steps.title: Solved example 1 — charge
steps.body: A current of 0.5 A flows through a bulb for 10 minutes. Q = I × t = 0.5 × 600 = **300 C**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — number of electrons
steps.body: How many electrons make up 1 C? n = 1/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = **6.25 × 10¹⁸**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using minutes instead of seconds in I = Q/t.
- Connecting the ammeter in parallel.
- Saying conventional current flows in the same direction as electrons.

activity.prompt: A charge of 240 C passes through a wire in 2 minutes. Find the current.

quiz.q: SI unit of current:
quiz.why: The SI unit of current is the ampere. 1 A = 1 C/s.

quiz.q: An ammeter is connected
quiz.why: An ammeter is connected in series so that the current to be measured passes through it.

quiz.q: Charge on one electron:
quiz.why: The charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C in magnitude.

quiz.q: Q for 0.5 A for 10 min:
Conventional current flows
options: from + to − in the external circuit
quiz.why: By convention, current flows from the positive to the negative terminal in the external circuit. Electrons move the opposite way.

scenes.text: Water flows from a high tank to a low tap because of a pressure difference.
Charges flow in a wire because of an electric 'pressure' difference — potential difference — made by a cell.
Georg Simon Ohm found that for a wire, current grows in step with that potential difference.

steps.title: Potential difference
steps.body:
**Potential difference V** between two points = work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other: **V = W/Q**.

- SI unit: **volt (V)**; 1 V = 1 J/C.
- **Voltmeter** measures potential difference; connected **in parallel** across the component.

steps.title: Ohm's law
steps.body:
At constant temperature, the current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends: **V ∝ I**, i.e. **V = IR**.

**R** is the **resistance**, unit **ohm (Ω)**; 1 Ω = 1 V/A. The V–I graph for a conductor obeying Ohm's law is a **straight line through the origin**; its slope (V/I) is R.

A **rheostat** (variable resistance) is used to change current in a circuit.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — work done
steps.body: Work to move 2 C of charge across a potential difference of 12 V: W = VQ = **24 J**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — resistance of a bulb
steps.body: An electric bulb draws 0.5 A from a 220 V supply. R = V/I = 220/0.5 = **440 Ω**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — new current
steps.body: A heater of resistance 100 Ω is connected to 220 V: I = **2.2 A**. If the voltage falls to 110 V, I = **1.1 A** (Ohm's law, same R).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Connecting the voltmeter in series.
- Using Ohm's law for a filament lamp whose temperature changes a lot (it is approximately true only at constant temperature).
- Writing R = IV.

activity.label: Slide the voltage across a 10 Ω resistor and read the current (I = V/R).

bands.text: Up to 1.2 A — e.g. 12 V gives 1.2 A.
Up to 2.4 A — doubling V doubles I (Ohm's law).

quiz.q: SI unit of potential difference:
quiz.why: The SI unit of potential difference is the volt, where 1 V = 1 J/C.

quiz.q: Ohm's law:
quiz.why: Ohm's law states V = IR, at constant temperature.

quiz.q: A voltmeter is connected
quiz.why: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is measured.

quiz.q: Bulb drawing 0.5 A at 220 V has resistance
The V–I graph for an ohmic conductor is
options: a straight line through the origin
quiz.why: For an ohmic conductor V is proportional to I, so the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin.

quiz.q: Work to move 3 C across 6 V:
quiz.why: Work W = V × Q = 6 × 3 = 18 J.

story.title: Why are heater coils made of nichrome?

scenes.text: An electric heater coil glows red-hot, but the copper connecting wires stay cool.
The coil is a long, thin wire of nichrome; the cord is thick copper.
Material, length and thickness decide resistance.

steps.title: Factors affecting resistance
steps.body:
The resistance of a uniform conductor:

- is **directly proportional to its length** (R ∝ l),
- is **inversely proportional to its area of cross-section** (R ∝ 1/A),
- depends on the **material** and **temperature**.

**R = ρ l / A**, where **ρ (rho) is resistivity**, SI unit **Ω m**. Resistivity is a property of the material (it changes with temperature, not with shape).

- Metals and alloys: very low ρ (10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m) — good conductors (silver, copper, aluminium are best).
- **Alloys** (nichrome, manganin, constantan) have higher ρ than their metals and do not oxidise easily at high temperature — used in heating devices.
- Insulators (rubber, glass): 10¹² to 10¹⁷ Ω m.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — change length and area
steps.body: A wire has resistance R. (a) Length doubled → **2R**. (b) Area doubled → **R/2**. (c) Diameter halved → area becomes 1/4 → **4R**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — stretch a wire
steps.body: A wire is stretched to double its length; its volume stays the same, so its area halves. New R = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = **4R**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — compute ρ
steps.body: A wire 2 m long with cross-section 1 × 10⁻⁷ m² has R = 20 Ω. ρ = RA/l = 20 × 10⁻⁷ / 2 = **1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m** (similar to nichrome).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying resistivity depends on the length of the wire (it depends only on material and temperature).
- Forgetting that halving the diameter quarters the area.
- Using copper for heater elements (too low resistivity, and it oxidises).

statements.s: Doubling the length of a wire doubles its resistance.
Resistivity of a wire changes if you cut it in half.
Copper is used for electrical transmission lines because of its low resistivity.
Alloys are used in heaters because they have low resistivity.
statements.why: They have high resistivity and resist oxidation.

statements.s: A thicker wire of the same material and length has less resistance.

quiz.q: SI unit of resistivity:
quiz.why: From ρ = RA/l, the SI unit of resistivity is the ohm metre (Ω m).

quiz.q: If the diameter of a wire is halved, its resistance becomes
quiz.why: Halving the diameter makes the area one-fourth, and R ∝ 1/A, so resistance becomes 4 times.

quiz.q: Heating elements are made of
quiz.why: Heating elements are made of alloys like nichrome, which have high resistivity and a high melting point.

quiz.q: Resistivity depends on
quiz.why: Resistivity depends on the material and temperature, not on length, area or shape.

quiz.q: A wire stretched to twice its length has resistance
quiz.why: Stretching to twice the length halves the area, so R becomes 2 × 2 = 4R.

story.title: Why aren't house lights in series?

scenes.text: Old festive light strings went dark entirely when one bulb failed.
In homes, when one bulb fuses, the fan keeps running.
Strings were in series; homes are wired in parallel. The maths explains why.

steps.title: Series
steps.body:
Resistors joined end to end: the **same current** flows through each; the total p.d. divides.

**Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃** (greater than the largest)

V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃. If one breaks, the whole circuit stops.

steps.title: Parallel
steps.body:
Resistors connected between the same two points: the **same p.d.** across each; current divides.

**1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃** (less than the smallest)

I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃. Each appliance gets the full voltage and can be switched independently — so **household circuits are parallel**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — series
steps.body: 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 15 Ω in series with 30 V. Rₛ = 30 Ω, I = 30/30 = **1 A**. Potential drops: **5 V, 10 V, 15 V**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — parallel
steps.body: 5 Ω, 10 Ω, 30 Ω in parallel across 12 V. 1/Rₚ = 6/30 + 3/30 + 1/30 = 10/30 → Rₚ = **3 Ω**. Total I = 12/3 = **4 A**; branch currents 2.4 A, 1.2 A, 0.4 A (they add to 4 A).

steps.title: Solved example 3 — mixed
steps.body: Two 4 Ω resistors in parallel (= 2 Ω) in series with a 3 Ω resistor: total = **5 Ω**. With 10 V, I = 2 A; the parallel pair has 4 V across it, so each 4 Ω carries 1 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding resistances directly for a parallel combination.
- Forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end (1/Rₚ = 1/3 means Rₚ = 3 Ω).
- Saying current is the same in parallel branches.

activity.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance of 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel.

quiz.q: In series, which quantity is the same in every resistor?
quiz.why: In a series circuit there is a single path, so the same current flows through every resistor.

quiz.q: Equivalent of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, 5 Ω in series:
quiz.why: In series, resistances add: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω.

quiz.q: Equivalent of two 10 Ω resistors in parallel:
quiz.why: Two equal resistors in parallel give R/2 = 10/2 = 5 Ω.

quiz.q: Household appliances are connected in
quiz.why: Appliances are connected in parallel so that each gets the full supply voltage and can be switched on or off independently.

quiz.q: Total current in example 2:
quiz.why: In example 2 the total current is the supply voltage divided by the equivalent resistance, 12/3 = 4 A.

quiz.q: Equivalent resistance in parallel is
quiz.why: The equivalent resistance in parallel is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

scenes.text: Mr Sharma's bill shows 300 units this month. A unit is 1 kWh.
His geyser, iron and heater convert electrical energy into heat.
Knowing power and energy helps you read the bill and save money.

steps.title: Joule's law of heating
steps.body:
Heat produced in a resistor: **H = I²Rt** (= VIt).

Heat is directly proportional to the **square of current**, to resistance and to time.

**Uses:** electric iron, toaster, oven, kettle, heater; **bulb filaments** (tungsten, melting point 3380 °C; bulbs filled with inert nitrogen/argon); **fuse** — a wire of an alloy with a suitable melting point (e.g. aluminium, copper, iron, lead) in series with the circuit, which **melts** when current exceeds a safe value and breaks the circuit. Fuse ratings: 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A etc.

steps.title: Electric power and energy
steps.body:
**Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R**; unit **watt (W)**; 1 W = 1 V × 1 A.

**Energy = P × t**. Commercial unit: **kilowatt hour (kWh)** = 1 unit = **3.6 × 10⁶ J**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — heat
steps.body: A 4 Ω heater carries 5 A for 2 minutes. H = I²Rt = 25 × 4 × 120 = **12,000 J**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — electric iron
steps.body: A 1100 W iron runs on 220 V. I = P/V = **5 A**; R = V/I = **44 Ω**. So the circuit needs a fuse rated a little above 5 A; heavy appliances are placed on the 15 A power circuit.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — cost
steps.body: A 1000 W heater runs 2 hours a day for 30 days: energy = 1 kW × 60 h = **60 kWh**. At ₹6 per unit, cost = **₹360**.

steps.title: Saving energy
steps.body: LED bulbs use much less power than incandescent bulbs for the same light. Switch off appliances at the plug, choose star-rated appliances, and do not overload sockets — overloading heats wires and can start fires.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using P = I²R when V is known and I is not (use P = V²/R).
- Confusing kW (power) with kWh (energy).
- Thinking a fuse is connected in parallel.

questions.why: A straight-line V–I graph means V is proportional to I, which verifies Ohm's law.

questions.q: Two bulbs 100 W and 60 W (both 220 V) are connected in parallel to 220 V. Total current:
questions.why: In parallel each bulb uses its own power, so total power = 100 + 60 = 160 W. I = P/V = 160/220 ≈ 0.73 A.

questions.q: An electric oven of 2 kW is used on a 220 V line with a 5 A fuse. What happens?
