The oven runs at half power safely
questions.why: The current is I = P/V = 2000/220 ≈ 9.1 A, which is more than the 5 A rating. The fuse melts and breaks the circuit.

questions.q: A wire's resistance is R. It is melted and drawn into a wire three times as long. New resistance:
questions.why: Drawing the wire three times as long makes its area one-third, since the volume stays the same. R ∝ l/A becomes 3 × 3 = 9 times, so 9R.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
courses.summary: Magnetic fields and field lines, the field around a straight wire, a circular loop and a solenoid, electromagnets, the force on a current-carrying conductor with Fleming's left-hand rule, and safe domestic electric circuits.
outcomes: Learners can describe magnetic field lines and their properties
Learners can use the right-hand thumb rule for straight wires, loops and solenoids
Learners can explain how an electromagnet is made and what affects its strength
Learners can apply Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of force
Learners can explain live, neutral and earth wires, fuses, short circuits and overloading

lessons.title: Magnetic field and field lines

scenes.text: In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle deflect when current flowed in a nearby wire.
Electricity and magnetism turned out to be linked.
To picture a magnetic field we draw field lines, using iron filings or a compass.

steps.title: Field lines
steps.body:
A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where its force can be felt. It has both **magnitude and direction**. A compass needle (a small magnet) points along the field.

**Properties of field lines:**
- They emerge from the **north pole** and merge at the **south pole** outside the magnet; inside the magnet they go from south to north — so they are **closed curves**.
- The **closer** the lines, the **stronger** the field (crowded near the poles).
- **Two field lines never cross** — otherwise a compass at the crossing would point in two directions at once.

Iron filings sprinkled on paper over a bar magnet arrange themselves along the field lines.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — why never cross?
steps.body: At any point the field has one direction. If two lines crossed, there would be two directions at that point, which is impossible.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — where is it strongest?
steps.body: Near the poles of a bar magnet field lines are crowded, so the field is strongest there.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying field lines start at S and end at N outside the magnet.
- Drawing field lines that cross.
- Saying field lines are open curves.

statements.s: Magnetic field lines are closed curves.
statements.why: N to S outside, S to N inside.

statements.s: Two field lines can intersect.
statements.why: The field would have two directions.

statements.s: Field lines are crowded where the field is strong.
Oersted showed that current produces a magnetic field.
Outside a magnet, field lines go from south to north.
statements.why: They go from north to south.

quiz.q: Outside a magnet, field lines go from
quiz.why: By convention, outside the magnet field lines run from the north pole to the south pole.

quiz.q: Field strength is shown by
quiz.why: Where field lines are closer together the magnetic field is stronger.

quiz.q: The scientist who found the magnetic effect of current:
quiz.why: Hans Christian Oersted found in 1820 that an electric current produces a magnetic effect.

quiz.q: A compass needle is
quiz.why: A compass needle is a small bar magnet that aligns itself along the magnetic field.

quiz.q: Magnetic field has
quiz.why: A magnetic field has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector quantity.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Magnetic Effects of Electric Current)

lessons.title: Fields of a straight wire, a loop and a solenoid

scenes.text: Kabir grips an imaginary wire with his right hand, thumb along the current.
His curled fingers show which way the magnetic field circles the wire.
Coil the wire into a loop or a long spring-like solenoid, and the field becomes stronger and more useful.

steps.title: Straight conductor
steps.body:
Field lines are **concentric circles** around the wire. Field strength **increases with current** and **decreases with distance** from the wire.

**Right-hand thumb rule:** hold the wire in your right hand with the **thumb along the current**; the **fingers curl in the direction of the field lines**. (Reversing current reverses the field — the compass deflects the other way.)

steps.title: Circular loop and solenoid
steps.body:
- **Circular loop:** near the wire the lines are circles; at the **centre** they become nearly **straight**. The field at the centre increases with current and with the **number of turns** n (fields of all turns add up) and decreases with larger radius.
- **Solenoid:** a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely like a cylinder. Its field pattern is like that of a **bar magnet**, with one end N and the other S. **Inside**, the field lines are **parallel straight lines** — the field is **uniform**.
- **Electromagnet:** a soft iron core placed inside a solenoid becomes strongly magnetised while current flows. Strength increases with more turns, more current and a soft-iron core. Used in cranes, electric bells, MRI-like equipment and relays.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — find the field direction
steps.body: Current flows vertically upward in a wire. Using the right-hand thumb rule (thumb up), the field lines seen from above circle **anticlockwise**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — make it stronger
steps.body: To strengthen a solenoid's field: increase the current, increase the number of turns, and insert a soft iron core.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the left hand for the thumb rule.
- Saying the field inside a solenoid is non-uniform.
- Using steel instead of soft iron for a temporary electromagnet (steel stays magnetised).

activity.prompt: Will the change make the magnetic field at the centre of a coil stronger or weaker?

items.text: Increase the radius of the loop
Move the compass farther from a straight wire

quiz.q: Field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are
quiz.why: The magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles around the wire.

quiz.q: The field inside a long solenoid is
quiz.why: Inside a long solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines, so the field is uniform.

quiz.q: Direction of field around a wire is given by
quiz.why: The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire.

quiz.q: A solenoid behaves like a
quiz.why: A solenoid carrying current behaves like a bar magnet, with a north and a south end.

quiz.q: Core used for an electromagnet:
quiz.why: Soft iron is used as the core of an electromagnet because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised.

quiz.q: Field at the centre of a loop increases with
quiz.why: The field at the centre of a coil increases with the number of turns, since the fields of the turns add up.

lessons.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor

scenes.text: An aluminium rod hangs between the poles of a horseshoe magnet.
When current flows through it, the rod swings out sideways; reversing current makes it swing the other way.
A magnet exerts a force on a current. Fleming's left hand tells the direction.

steps.title: The force
steps.body:
A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a **force** (André-Marie Ampère suggested the magnet must exert an equal and opposite force on the conductor).

- The force is **largest when the current is perpendicular** to the field; it is zero when they are parallel.
- Reversing either the current or the field reverses the force.

**Fleming's left-hand rule:** stretch the **thumb, forefinger and middle finger** of the **left hand** mutually perpendicular. **Forefinger → field**, **middle finger → current**, then **thumb → force (motion)**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — apply the rule
steps.body: Current flows towards the east in a wire placed in a magnetic field pointing north (horizontal). Forefinger north, middle finger east → thumb points **upward**: the force is vertically up.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — electron beam
steps.body: An electron beam moving west is like a conventional current towards the **east**. In a downward magnetic field, the force on it (by the left-hand rule) is found with forefinger down and middle finger east: the thumb points **north**, so the beam deflects north.

steps.title: Where it is used
steps.body: Electric motors, loudspeakers, electric fans, washing machines and mixers use this force. Inside the human body, weak currents in nerves create very small magnetic fields; **MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)** uses strong magnetic fields to make images of internal organs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the right hand for the force.
- Forgetting that electron flow is opposite to conventional current.
- Saying force is maximum when current is parallel to the field.

activity.prompt: Fleming's left-hand rule: match each finger with the quantity.

quiz.q: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of
options: force on a current-carrying conductor in a field
quiz.why: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

quiz.q: The force is maximum when current and field are
quiz.why: The force is maximum when the current is perpendicular to the field, since the force depends on sin of the angle between them.

quiz.q: Reversing the current in the rod makes the force
quiz.why: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force on the rod.

quiz.q: In the left-hand rule, the forefinger shows
quiz.why: In the left-hand rule the forefinger shows the field, the middle finger the current and the thumb the force.

quiz.q: A device using this force:
quiz.why: An electric fan motor works on this force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Heaters, fuses and bulbs do not.

lessons.title: Domestic electric circuits

scenes.text: During Diwali, Riya's family plugs a heater, an iron and lights into one socket. Suddenly the power goes off.
The MCB in the meter box has tripped — it sensed too much current.
Domestic wiring has built-in safety: fuses, MCBs and the earth wire.

steps.title: Supply and wires
steps.body:
In India, mains supply is **AC at 220 V and 50 Hz**.

- **Live (phase) wire:** usually **red** (or brown in newer wiring) insulation — at high potential.
- **Neutral wire:** **black** (or blue).
- **Earth wire:** **green** (or green-yellow) — connected to a metal plate deep in the ground near the house.

The supply passes through the electricity meter and the **main fuse/MCB**. There are usually two circuits: a **5 A** circuit for lights and fans and a **15 A** circuit for heavy appliances (geysers, ACs, coolers). Appliances are connected **in parallel** so each gets 220 V and can be switched on or off independently.

steps.title: Safety devices and faults
steps.body:
- **Earthing:** the metal body of appliances (iron, toaster, fridge) is connected to the earth wire. If the live wire touches the body, current flows to earth (a low-resistance path), protecting the user from severe shock.
- **Short circuit:** live and neutral wires come into direct contact (damaged insulation or a fault) — current rises sharply.
- **Overloading:** too many appliances on one socket, or a sudden voltage increase — current exceeds the safe value.
- **Fuse / MCB** in series with the live wire melts or trips in such cases, cutting off supply and preventing fires and damage.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — why parallel?
steps.body: In parallel, each appliance gets the full 220 V, has its own switch, and if one fails, the others keep working. In series, the current would be the same for all and one failure would stop everything.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — overloading
steps.body: An oven (2 kW) and a geyser (2 kW) on one 220 V, 5 A circuit draw about 4000/220 ≈ 18 A — far more than 5 A. The fuse would blow; heavy appliances belong on the 15 A circuit, and should not run together on one socket.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the fuse in the neutral wire.
- Using a thick copper wire in place of a fuse wire ('to stop it blowing') — this removes protection and can cause fires.
- Thinking the earth wire carries current all the time.
- Touching switches with wet hands.

activity.prompt: Home electrical safety checklist:
items: Do not plug many heavy appliances into one socket
Use 3-pin plugs with earthing for metal-bodied appliances
Never replace a fuse with a thick copper wire
Switch off the main supply before any repair

quiz.q: Potential difference of domestic supply in India:
quiz.why: The domestic supply in India is 220 V, alternating at 50 Hz.

quiz.q: Colour of the earth wire (traditional):
quiz.why: The earth wire traditionally has green insulation, though green-yellow is also used.

quiz.q: A fuse is connected in
quiz.why: A fuse is connected in series with the live wire, so that it breaks the live path when the current is too high.

quiz.q: Short circuit happens when
quiz.why: A short circuit happens when the live and neutral wires touch directly, giving a very low resistance path and a very large current.

quiz.q: Earthing protects by
options: giving leakage current a low-resistance path to the ground
quiz.why: Earthing gives any leakage current a low-resistance path to the ground, so the user does not get a shock.

quiz.q: Heavy appliances like geysers are put on
quiz.why: Heavy appliances such as geysers draw a large current, so they are connected to the 15 A circuit.

sources: NCERT Class 10 Science (Magnetic Effects of Electric Current)

questions.q: Inside a bar magnet, field lines go from
questions.why: Inside a bar magnet the field lines run from the south pole to the north pole, so they form closed loops.

questions.q: The rule for the direction of field around a straight wire:
questions.why: The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire.

questions.q: Domestic supply frequency in India:
questions.why: The AC supply in India has a frequency of 50 Hz.

questions.q: Wire with red/brown insulation is the
questions.why: Red (or brown) insulation marks the live wire, which carries the current into the appliance.

questions.q: A strong electromagnet needs a core of
questions.why: A strong electromagnet needs a soft-iron core, since soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised.

questions.q: Two field lines never intersect because
options: the field has only one direction at a point
questions.why: Two field lines never cross because the field has only one direction at any point. If they crossed, there would be two directions at the crossing.

questions.q: Assertion: The field inside a long solenoid is uniform. Reason: field lines inside it are parallel straight lines.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Inside a long solenoid the lines are parallel and equally spaced, which means the field is uniform.

questions.q: Field strength near a straight wire increases when
questions.why: The field near a straight wire increases when the current increases, since B is proportional to I. It decreases with distance.

questions.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule the thumb shows
questions.why: In Fleming's left-hand rule the thumb shows the force or motion.

questions.q: Case: In a house, the MCB trips every time the heater and iron are switched on together. The cause is
questions.why: A heater and an iron together draw a large current. The MCB trips because the circuit is overloaded.

questions.q: Case continued: a safe solution is to
options: use the appliances one at a time or on a proper 15 A circuit
replace the MCB with copper wire
questions.why: Using the appliances one at a time, or on a proper 15 A circuit, avoids overloading. Removing earthing or replacing the MCB with copper wire is dangerous.

questions.q: A current-carrying wire placed along the direction of a magnetic field experiences
questions.why: A wire parallel to the field experiences no force, because the force depends on sin of the angle between current and field, which is zero.

questions.q: A horizontal wire carries current from south to north in a vertically upward field. The force on it is towards the
questions.why: Forefinger up (field), middle finger north (current). By the left-hand rule the thumb points east, which is the direction of the force.

questions.q: Why is a fuse wire made of a material with a low melting point?
options: So it melts quickly when excess current heats it
To increase resistance of the circuit
questions.why: A fuse wire has a low melting point so that it melts quickly when excess current heats it, breaking the circuit.

questions.q: Total current drawn by a 2 kW geyser and a 1.3 kW heater together on 220 V:
An electron moving north enters a magnetic field directed vertically downward. The force on it is towards the
questions.why: Conventional current south; forefinger down, middle finger south → thumb points east.

questions.q: Which change does NOT increase the strength of an electromagnet?
options: Replacing the soft-iron core with a wooden core
questions.why: A wooden core is not magnetic, so replacing the soft-iron core with wood weakens the electromagnet. More current, more turns and a soft-iron core strengthen it.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Our Environment
courses.summary: Ecosystems and their components, food chains and food webs, trophic levels and the 10% law of energy flow, biological magnification, ozone layer depletion, and managing the garbage we produce.
outcomes: Learners can identify biotic and abiotic components and types of ecosystems
Learners can build food chains and food webs and name trophic levels
Learners can apply the 10% law to energy flow
Learners can explain biological magnification with an example
Learners can explain ozone formation and depletion and suggest waste-management steps

scenes.text: Class 10-B sets up an aquarium with fish, water plants, snails, sand and light.
The fish eat, plants make food, snails clean up — the tank becomes a small, self-supporting world.
That is a mini ecosystem: living and non-living parts interacting.

steps.title: What is an ecosystem?
steps.body:
An **ecosystem** consists of all the living organisms in an area together with the non-living parts of the environment, interacting with each other.

- **Biotic components:** plants, animals, microorganisms.
- **Abiotic components:** temperature, rainfall, wind, soil, minerals, water, light.

**Natural** ecosystems: forests, ponds, lakes, grasslands. **Artificial (human-made)**: gardens, crop fields, aquariums.

steps.title: Roles of organisms
steps.body:
- **Producers:** green plants and blue-green algae make food by photosynthesis.
- **Consumers:** depend on producers directly or indirectly — **herbivores**, **carnivores**, **omnivores**, **parasites**.
- **Decomposers:** bacteria and fungi break down dead remains and wastes into simple substances that return to the soil — they **recycle nutrients**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — aquarium cleaning
steps.body: Why don't we clean ponds and lakes the way we clean an aquarium? Natural ecosystems have **decomposers** that break down wastes; an aquarium, being small and artificial, lacks enough decomposers.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — what if decomposers vanished?
steps.body: Dead plants and animals would pile up and nutrients would not return to the soil; producers would run short of minerals, and the whole ecosystem would suffer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a crop field a natural ecosystem.
- Saying decomposers are producers.
- Forgetting abiotic factors (light, water, temperature) are part of the ecosystem.

activity.prompt: Biotic or abiotic component?

quiz.q: An artificial ecosystem:
quiz.why: A crop field is made by humans, so it is an artificial ecosystem. Forests, ponds and deserts are natural.

quiz.q: Decomposers include
quiz.why: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi, which break down dead remains.

quiz.q: Producers are
quiz.why: Producers are green plants that make food by photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Which is abiotic?
quiz.why: Temperature is a non-living part of the environment, so it is abiotic. Fish, algae and mushrooms are living.

quiz.q: Decomposers help by
quiz.why: Decomposers break down dead organisms and recycle nutrients to the soil, where plants can use them again.

lessons.title: Food chains, food webs and energy flow

scenes.text: In a forest, deer eat grass, and a tiger eats the deer.
The energy in the tiger's muscles began as sunlight caught by grass.
But at each step, most energy is lost — which is why there are far fewer tigers than deer.

steps.title: Food chains and trophic levels
steps.body:
A **food chain** is a series of organisms eating one another: grass → deer → lion; grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.

Each step is a **trophic level**:
- 1st: **producers** (autotrophs)
- 2nd: **herbivores / primary consumers**
- 3rd: **small carnivores / secondary consumers**
- 4th: **large carnivores / tertiary consumers**

In nature, food chains interlink to form a **food web** (an organism may be eaten by many others).

steps.title: Energy flow
steps.body:
- Green plants capture about **1%** of the sunlight falling on leaves and convert it to food energy.
- **10% law:** only about **10%** of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next as organic matter; the rest is used for life processes and lost as heat.
- So food chains usually have only **3–4 trophic levels**; there are fewer organisms at higher levels.
- Energy flow is **unidirectional**: energy captured by autotrophs does not go back to the Sun, and energy passed to herbivores does not return to plants.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — 10% law
steps.body: Producers in a field store 10,000 J. Herbivores get **1000 J**, small carnivores **100 J**, large carnivores **10 J**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 — why eat plants?
steps.body: A vegetarian diet uses energy at the 2nd trophic level, so more energy from the same farmland is available to people than if plants are first fed to animals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 10% of energy is lost (it is 90% lost; 10% passes on).
- Drawing arrows from consumer to food (arrows point in the direction of energy flow: food → eater).
- Saying energy cycles back to producers.

activity.prompt: If producers fix 20,000 J of energy, how much reaches the third trophic level (small carnivores)?

quiz.q: Organisms at the first trophic level:
quiz.why: Producers are at the first trophic level of a food chain.

quiz.q: According to the 10% law, energy passed to the next level is about
quiz.why: By the 10% law only about 10% of the energy passes to the next trophic level. The rest is lost.

quiz.q: Energy flow in an ecosystem is
quiz.why: Energy flow in an ecosystem is one-way, from the Sun to producers and then to consumers. It is not recycled.

quiz.q: Herbivores occupy the
quiz.why: Herbivores eat producers, so they are at the second trophic level.

quiz.q: Food chains are short because
options: energy decreases sharply at each level
quiz.why: Food chains are short because energy falls sharply (about 10% passes on) at each level, so little is left for higher levels.

quiz.q: Plants convert about what fraction of incident sunlight into food energy?
quiz.why: Plants capture only about 1% of the sunlight that falls on them as food energy.

scenes.text: Farmers spray a pesticide on crops; rain washes some into a pond.
Tiny amounts enter plankton, then small fish, then big fish, then the birds and people who eat them.
At every step the chemical concentrates more. This is biological magnification.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
Some harmful chemicals (e.g. many pesticides) are **non-biodegradable** — they are not broken down and are not excreted easily. When they enter a food chain, they **accumulate progressively at each trophic level**.

Since **humans** often occupy the top level, the **maximum concentration** can build up in our bodies. Such chemicals have been found in food grains, fruits, vegetables, meat and even milk.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — compare concentrations
steps.body: Pesticide concentration in a pond chain: water (low) < plankton < small fish < large fish < fish-eating birds (highest).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — reduce the risk
steps.body: Use pesticides only as recommended, prefer integrated pest management and biodegradable alternatives, wash fruits and vegetables well, and support safe disposal of chemicals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying energy and chemicals both decrease up the chain (energy decreases; non-biodegradable chemicals increase).
- Thinking only animals at the top are affected (all levels absorb some).
- Confusing biological magnification with the 10% law.

activity.prompt: Order the organisms from lowest to highest pesticide concentration.

quiz.q: Biological magnification means
options: increase in energy up the chain
increase in concentration of harmful chemicals along a food chain
quiz.why: Biological magnification is the increase in concentration of harmful chemicals as they pass along a food chain.

quiz.q: Maximum concentration of pesticides is found in
quiz.why: Harmful chemicals build up along a food chain, so the highest concentration is found in the top consumers.

quiz.q: Chemicals that show magnification are usually
quiz.why: Chemicals that show biological magnification are non-biodegradable, so they are not broken down and stay in the body.

quiz.q: Humans are at risk because they
options: often occupy the top trophic level
quiz.why: Humans often feed at the top trophic level, so they may take in large amounts of accumulated chemicals.

quiz.q: A way to reduce biological magnification:
options: use pesticides only as needed and prefer biodegradable alternatives
quiz.why: Using pesticides only when needed and choosing biodegradable alternatives reduces the chemicals entering the food chain.

scenes.text: High above us, a thin layer of ozone shields life from the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays.
In the 1980s scientists found it thinning, mainly due to CFCs from old refrigerators and aerosol sprays.
Global action and our daily choices about waste both shape the planet we live on.

steps.title: Ozone
steps.body:
Ozone (O₃) is a molecule of three oxygen atoms. At ground level it is a deadly poison, but in the **upper atmosphere** it **shields** the Earth from **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**, which can cause skin cancer and damage living things.

**Formation:** UV radiation splits O₂ into free oxygen atoms: O₂ → O + O; then O + O₂ → O₃.

**Depletion:** a sharp drop was noticed from the 1980s, linked to synthetic chemicals like **chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)** used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers. In **1987**, the **United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)** reached an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels; CFC-free refrigerators are now standard.

steps.title: Managing garbage
steps.body:
- **Biodegradable** substances can be broken down by biological processes (vegetable peels, paper, cotton, leaves, dung).
- **Non-biodegradable** substances are not broken down this way (plastics, glass, metals, many pesticides); they persist and harm ecosystems.

**Good practice:** segregate waste at home (wet/biodegradable and dry/non-biodegradable), compost kitchen waste, reduce single-use plastic, reuse and recycle, carry a cloth bag. Disposable cups, packaging and changed lifestyles create more waste; switching from paper cups to kulhads at a large scale would also need clay and topsoil — every choice has trade-offs.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — classify
steps.body: Banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth → biodegradable. Plastic bottle, glass jar, aluminium can → non-biodegradable (but recyclable).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — explain
steps.body: Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern? More UV radiation would reach the Earth, increasing skin cancer, cataracts and harming plants and aquatic life.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ozone is helpful at ground level (it is harmful there).
- Calling all plastics biodegradable.
- Saying CFCs were banned by a 1997 treaty (the UNEP agreement was in 1987).

activity.prompt: Biodegradable or non-biodegradable?

quiz.q: Ozone protects us from
quiz.why: The ozone layer protects living things from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation of the Sun.

quiz.q: Main cause of ozone depletion:
quiz.why: CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) from refrigerators and aerosols are the main cause of ozone depletion.

quiz.q: Ozone forms when
options: O atoms combine with O₂ molecules
quiz.why: Ozone forms when UV light splits O₂ into oxygen atoms, which combine with O₂ molecules: O + O₂ → O₃.

quiz.q: UNEP agreement to freeze CFC production was in
quiz.why: In 1987 UNEP reached an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels.

quiz.q: A non-biodegradable substance:
quiz.why: Plastic is non-biodegradable, so it persists in the environment. Fruit peel, paper and cotton are biodegradable.

quiz.q: Best way to handle kitchen waste:
quiz.why: Kitchen waste is biodegradable, so composting it returns nutrients to the soil.

questions.q: A natural ecosystem:
questions.why: A pond is a natural ecosystem. A garden, an aquarium and a crop field are made by humans.

questions.q: Decomposers are
questions.why: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi, which break down dead organisms and wastes.

questions.q: Ozone is made of
questions.why: Ozone is O₃, a molecule made of three oxygen atoms. Ordinary oxygen, O₂, has two.

questions.q: Which is biodegradable?
questions.why: Paper is biodegradable because microbes can break it down. Glass, aluminium and plastic are not broken down easily.

questions.q: In grass → deer → tiger, the tiger is a
options: secondary consumer (top carnivore) at the 3rd trophic level
questions.why: In grass → deer → tiger, grass is the first level, deer the second and tiger the third. The tiger eats a herbivore, so it is a secondary consumer and the top carnivore.

questions.q: If a herbivore gets 1000 J, the next carnivore gets about
questions.why: By the 10% law only about 10% of energy passes to the next level, so 10% of 1000 J = 100 J.

questions.q: Assertion: Energy flow in ecosystems is unidirectional. Reason: energy captured by autotrophs does not revert to the Sun.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Energy captured by autotrophs flows to consumers and is lost as heat. It never returns to the Sun, so the flow is one-way.

questions.q: CFCs were widely used as
questions.why: CFCs were widely used as refrigerants in refrigerators and air conditioners, and in aerosol sprays.

questions.q: Which food chain is correct?
questions.why: Energy flows from the food to the eater, so a chain starts with a producer: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.

questions.q: Case: A pond near farms has a fish-eating bird population with thin, fragile eggshells. Tests show high pesticide levels in birds but low levels in water. This is
questions.why: High pesticide levels in birds at the top of the food chain but low levels in the water show that the chemicals build up along the chain. This is biological magnification.

questions.q: Case continued: which organism in the pond would show the LOWEST pesticide concentration?
questions.why: The pesticide concentration rises up the food chain, so the lowest is in plankton and algae at the first trophic level.

questions.q: Why are there usually not more than four trophic levels?
options: Energy available becomes too little after a few levels
questions.why: Each step passes on only about 10% of the energy, so after three or four levels too little is left to support another level.

questions.q: If 1% of 1,000,000 J of sunlight is fixed by plants, how much energy reaches primary consumers?
questions.why: 1% of 1,000,000 J is 10,000 J fixed by plants. Primary consumers get about 10% of that, which is 1000 J.

questions.q: Which step correctly shows ozone formation?
options: O₂ → O + O, then O + O₂ → O₃
questions.why: UV light splits an O₂ molecule into two O atoms, and each O atom then combines with another O₂ molecule: O + O₂ → O₃.

questions.q: Removing all frogs from a food web of grass → grasshopper → frog → snake would most likely
questions.why: Without frogs, the grasshoppers are not eaten and increase, while snakes lose their food and decrease.

questions.q: Why is changing from disposable paper cups to clay kulhads at a very large scale not a perfect solution?
options: Making kulhads on a large scale uses fertile topsoil and resources
questions.why: Making kulhads on a large scale uses fertile topsoil and resources. So every option has some environmental cost.

courses.title: Class 10 Science · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: One-page summaries of chemistry, biology and physics for all 13 chapters, key formulas and equations, exam strategy, and two full mock papers (as practice quizzes and a 24-question final test) with assertion–reason, case-based and numerical questions.
outcomes: Learners can recall key equations, definitions and formulas of all 13 chapters
Learners can answer mixed board-style questions under time pressure
Learners can solve physics numericals with correct signs and units
Learners can identify weak chapters and plan revision

scenes.text: The night before the exam, Neel writes every key chemical equation from memory.
Then he checks them here and corrects any slips.
Active recall beats rereading.

steps.title: Reactions (Ch 1)
steps.body:
- Combination: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat
- Decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (heat); 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (electricity); 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (light)
- Displacement: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu
- Double displacement: Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ (white) + 2NaCl
- Redox: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O
- Corrosion needs air + water; rancidity prevented by antioxidants, nitrogen, airtight storage

steps.title: Acids, bases, salts (Ch 2)
steps.body:
- Metal + acid → salt + H₂; carbonate + acid → salt + H₂O + CO₂; acid + base → salt + water
- pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic; tooth decay below 5.5; acid rain below 5.6
- Chlor-alkali: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂
- Bleaching powder CaOCl₂; baking soda NaHCO₃; washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; PoP CaSO₄·½H₂O; gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O; blue vitriol CuSO₄·5H₂O

steps.title: Metals and non-metals (Ch 3)
steps.body:
- Reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au
- Amphoteric oxides: Al₂O₃, ZnO
- Roasting (sulphide, excess air), calcination (carbonate, limited air), reduction with C; thermite Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃
- Electrolytic refining: impure anode, pure cathode, anode mud
- Alloys: brass Cu+Zn, bronze Cu+Sn, solder Pb+Sn; 22-carat gold

steps.title: Carbon compounds (Ch 4)
steps.body:
- Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂; homologous members differ by CH₂ (14 u)
- Suffixes: -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid; prefixes chloro-, bromo-
- Oxidation: ethanol → ethanoic acid (alk. KMnO₄ / acid. K₂Cr₂O₇)
- Addition: hydrogenation with Ni; substitution: CH₄ + Cl₂ (sunlight)
- Esterification: acid + alcohol (conc. H₂SO₄) → ester; saponification: ester + NaOH → soap/salt + alcohol
- Micelles; detergents work in hard water

steps.title: Top chemistry slips
steps.body:
- Unbalanced equations.
- PoP vs gypsum formula.
- Roasting vs calcination.
- Counting the –COOH carbon.

cards.front: Gas that turns lime water milky
pH below which tooth enamel corrodes

quiz.q: Washing soda formula:
quiz.why: Washing soda is sodium carbonate with 10 molecules of water of crystallisation: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

quiz.q: Which metal does not displace hydrogen from dilute acids?
quiz.why: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Zn, Fe and Mg can.

quiz.q: General formula of alkenes:
quiz.why: Alkenes have one double bond and the general formula CₙH₂ₙ.

quiz.q: Rusting needs
quiz.why: Rusting needs both air (oxygen) and water.

quiz.q: Bleaching powder is made by passing chlorine over
quiz.why: Bleaching powder is made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O.

scenes.text: Biology answers score high when key terms and sequences are exact.
Riya revises each process as a short sequence of steps.
Sequences are easy to recall and to write in exams.

steps.title: Life processes (Ch 5)
steps.body:
- Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O (light, chlorophyll)
- Digestion: mouth (amylase) → stomach (HCl, pepsin, mucus) → small intestine (bile, trypsin, lipase; villi absorb) → large intestine (water)
- Glucose → pyruvate (cytoplasm) → CO₂ + H₂O (mitochondria, O₂) / ethanol + CO₂ (yeast) / lactic acid (muscle)
- Heart: 4 chambers, double circulation; BP ~120/80 mm Hg
- Xylem (water, transpiration pull), phloem (food, ATP)
- Nephron: glomerulus filtration → tubular reabsorption → urine

steps.title: Control and coordination (Ch 6)
steps.body:
- Neuron: dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending → synapse (chemical)
- Reflex arc: receptor → sensory → relay (spinal cord) → motor → effector
- Cerebrum (thinking), cerebellum (balance), medulla (BP, salivation, vomiting)
- Plant hormones: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid
- Glands: pituitary (GH), thyroid (thyroxin, iodine), adrenal (adrenaline), pancreas (insulin), testes, ovaries; feedback control

steps.title: Reproduction and heredity (Ch 7–8)
steps.body:
- Fission (Amoeba, Plasmodium), fragmentation (Spirogyra), regeneration (Planaria), budding (Hydra, yeast), spores (Rhizopus), vegetative propagation
- Flower: pollination → pollen tube → fertilisation → ovule → seed, ovary → fruit
- Human: fertilisation in oviduct; placenta; menstruation if no fertilisation
- Contraception: barrier, hormonal, IUD, surgical; STIs
- Monohybrid F2 3 : 1 (1 : 2 : 1); dihybrid F2 9 : 3 : 3 : 1
- Sex: XX female, XY male; father's sperm decides

steps.title: Our environment (Ch 13)
steps.body:
- Trophic levels; 10% law; energy flow unidirectional
- Biological magnification of non-biodegradable chemicals
- Ozone: O₂ → O + O; O + O₂ → O₃; CFCs deplete it; UNEP 1987
- Segregate, compost, reduce, reuse, recycle

steps.title: Top biology slips
steps.body:
- Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.
- Ovule → seed, ovary → fruit.
- 10% passes on, 90% lost.
- Auxin moves to the shaded side.

activity.prompt: Match each process with where it happens.

quiz.q: Enzyme that digests proteins in the stomach:
quiz.why: Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach, in an acidic medium.

quiz.q: Balance is controlled by the
quiz.why: The cerebellum, part of the hindbrain, controls balance and posture.

quiz.q: F2 phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross:
quiz.why: The F2 phenotypic ratio of a dihybrid cross is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

quiz.q: Hormone deficient in diabetes:
quiz.why: Diabetes is due to too little insulin, made by the pancreas.

quiz.q: Energy transferred to the next trophic level:
quiz.why: About 10% of the energy is passed to the next trophic level, according to the 10% law.

scenes.text: Most physics marks are lost to sign errors and unit slips, not to forgotten formulas.
Ishaan makes a rule: write u, v, f with signs before substituting, and convert cm to m for power.
His numerical scores jump.

steps.title: Light (Ch 9)
steps.body:
- Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; m = −v/u; R = 2f; concave f < 0, convex f > 0
- Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; m = v/u; P = 1/f (m) in dioptres; convex P > 0, concave P < 0; P = P₁ + P₂
- n = c/v = sin i / sin r; air 1.0003, water 1.33, glass 1.52, diamond 2.42
- u is always negative (object on the left)

steps.title: Eye and colours (Ch 10)
steps.body:
- Near point 25 cm, far point infinity; accommodation by ciliary muscles
- Myopia → concave lens; hypermetropia → convex lens; presbyopia → bifocal
- VIBGYOR; violet deviates most, red least; rainbow opposite the Sun
- Twinkling, advance sunrise (~2 min) = atmospheric refraction; blue sky, red sunset = scattering

steps.title: Electricity (Ch 11)
steps.body:
- I = Q/t; V = W/Q; V = IR; R = ρl/A
- Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …
- H = I²Rt; P = VI = I²R = V²/R; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
- Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel

steps.title: Magnetic effects (Ch 12)
steps.body:
- Field lines: closed, never cross, crowded where strong
- Right-hand thumb rule (field around wire); solenoid like a bar magnet, uniform field inside
- Fleming's left-hand rule: forefinger field, middle finger current, thumb force
- Domestic: 220 V, 50 Hz; live, neutral, earth; fuse/MCB in live wire; 5 A and 15 A circuits

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body:
- First 15 minutes: read the whole paper and mark easy questions.
- For numericals: Given → Formula → Substitution with units → Answer with unit and sign meaning.
- Draw labelled diagrams with a pencil and ruler; label arrows on rays.
- Keep 10 minutes to check.

steps.title: Top physics slips
steps.body:
- m = −v/u (mirror) vs m = v/u (lens).
- f in metres for power.
- Parallel resistance: take the reciprocal at the end.
- Fleming's LEFT hand for force.

activity.prompt: Physics practice before the exam:
items: Solve 3 mirror and 3 lens numericals with signs
Compute one electricity bill in kWh
Practise the right-hand thumb rule and left-hand rule with real directions
Draw the ray diagrams for convex lens positions

quiz.q: Power of a lens with f = −25 cm:
quiz.why: P = 1/f = 1/(−0.25 m) = −4 D, negative for a concave lens.

quiz.q: Equivalent of 4 Ω and 4 Ω in parallel:
quiz.why: Two equal resistors in parallel give R/2 = 4/2 = 2 Ω.

quiz.q: Red light is used for danger signals because it
quiz.why: Red light has the longest wavelength and is scattered the least, so it can be seen from far away. That is why danger signals are red.

quiz.q: Magnification of a mirror:
quiz.why: The magnification for mirrors is m = −v/u. For lenses it is v/u.

quiz.q: Energy used by a 500 W appliance in 4 h:
quiz.why: Energy = power × time = 0.5 kW × 4 h = 2 kWh.

scenes.text: Set a 25-minute timer for these 8 questions.
Do rough work on paper as in the real exam.
Afterwards read every explanation, and note the chapter of each mistake.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body:
- 8 mixed questions from all 13 chapters.
- Work first on paper; then choose.
- Aim for 6/8 or more.

steps.title: Pacing
steps.body: About 3 minutes per question here. In the board exam, objective questions should take about a minute each to leave time for long answers.

steps.title: Honesty rule
steps.body: Do not look at the summaries during the mock — the goal is to find what you still need to learn.

activity.prompt: After Mock 1: which chapters caused mistakes, and what will you revise tomorrow?

quiz.q: Which is a decomposition reaction?
quiz.why: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ is a decomposition reaction, because one compound breaks into simpler substances.

quiz.q: A solution of pH 12 is
quiz.why: pH 12 is well above 7, so the solution is strongly basic.

quiz.q: Ionic compounds conduct electricity
quiz.why: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state or in solution, when their ions are free to move.

quiz.q: The blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart:
quiz.why: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. It is an exception, as other veins carry deoxygenated blood.

quiz.q: Growth of a pollen tube towards the ovule:
quiz.why: Growth of the pollen tube towards the ovule is a response to chemicals, so it is chemotropism.

quiz.q: A convex lens of f = 20 cm with an object at 40 cm forms an image at
quiz.why: With the object at 2F₁ (40 cm for f = 20 cm), a convex lens forms an image at 2F₂, which is 40 cm on the other side. Check: 1/v = 1/20 − 1/40 = 1/40.

quiz.q: Resistance of a 220 V, 100 W bulb:
A food chain with 10,000 J at producers gives the 3rd trophic level
quiz.why: Producers have 10,000 J. The second level gets 10% = 1000 J and the third gets 10% of that, which is 100 J.

scenes.text: A day after Mock 1 and revision, try this second paper.
Compare scores — improvement shows your revision is working.
Then attempt the 24-question final test of this course.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body:
- 8 new mixed questions, a little harder.
- 25 minutes; working on paper.
- Mark each question by chapter and by type (concept, numerical, application).

steps.title: When stuck
steps.body: Write what is given, draw a sketch, write the relevant law or formula — boards give step marks.

steps.title: Last-minute changes
steps.body: Avoid changing answers at the last minute without a clear reason.

activity.prompt: After Mock 2: what improved since Mock 1, and what is still weak?

quiz.q: In 2Pb(NO₃)₂ → 2PbO + 4NO₂ + O₂, the brown gas is
quiz.why: Heating lead nitrate gives brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide, NO₂.

quiz.q: Plaster of Paris sets into a hard mass because it
options: combines with water to form gypsum
quiz.why: Plaster of Paris combines with water to form crystals of gypsum, which makes it set into a hard mass.

quiz.q: An element with configuration 2, 8, 1 forms an ion with charge
quiz.why: An element with configuration 2, 8, 1 is sodium. It loses one electron to form an ion with charge +1.

quiz.q: In a monohybrid cross Tt × tt, the percentage of dwarf plants is
quiz.why: Tt × tt gives Tt and tt in a 1 : 1 ratio, so half (50%) are dwarf (tt).

quiz.q: A person with far point 1.5 m needs a lens of power about
quiz.why: For a far point of 1.5 m the lens has f = −1.5 m, so P = 1/f ≈ −0.67 D.

quiz.q: A concave mirror forms a real image 3 times the object size at 30 cm in front. Object distance:
quiz.why: m = −v/u. With m = −3 and v = −30 cm, −3 = 30/u, so u = −10 cm. The object is 10 cm from the mirror.

quiz.q: Three 2 Ω resistors in parallel connected to 2 V draw total current
quiz.why: Three 2 Ω resistors in parallel give 2/3 Ω. Current = V/R = 2 ÷ (2/3) = 3 A.

quiz.q: Direction of force on a conductor in a field is given by
quiz.why: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force on a conductor carrying current in a magnetic field.

questions.q: Balanced form of H₂ + O₂ → H₂O:
questions.why: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 4 H and 2 O on each side, so it is balanced.

questions.q: Litmus is extracted from
questions.why: Litmus is extracted from lichen, which is a natural indicator.

questions.q: Unit of power of a lens:
questions.why: The SI unit of lens power is the dioptre (D).

questions.q: Site of photosynthesis in a cell:
questions.why: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll.

questions.q: Number of chromosome pairs in human cells:
questions.why: Human cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes (22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes).

questions.q: Which metal is stored in kerosene?
questions.why: Sodium is highly reactive with air and water, so it is stored in kerosene.

questions.q: The image formed by a plane mirror is
questions.why: A plane mirror gives a virtual, erect image the same size as the object.

questions.q: Assertion: Detergents work in hard water. Reason: they do not form insoluble salts with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Detergents do not form insoluble salts (scum) with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so they work in hard water.

questions.q: Ethanol on heating with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K gives
questions.why: Heating ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K removes water (dehydration) and gives ethene.

questions.q: The force on a conductor is zero when current is
questions.why: The force is zero when the current is parallel to the field, because there is no component of the current across the field.

questions.q: A bulb of 60 W runs 5 hours daily for 30 days. Energy used:
Case: A student adds zinc granules to dilute HCl and collects the gas. A burning splinter gives a pop sound. The gas and equation are
questions.why: Zinc and dilute HCl give hydrogen, which burns with a pop sound: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

questions.q: Case continued: if copper turnings are used instead, the student observes
questions.why: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it does not react with dilute HCl and no gas is seen.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of the liver in digestion?
questions.why: Trypsin is made by the pancreas, not the liver. The liver makes bile, which emulsifies fats and makes food alkaline.

questions.q: The far point of a myopic eye is 50 cm. Power of the corrective lens:
questions.why: A far point of 50 cm needs a lens with f = −0.5 m. P = 1/f = −2 D.

questions.q: An object is placed 12 cm from a convex lens of f = 8 cm. Image distance:
Resistors 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series are connected in parallel with a 5 Ω resistor. Equivalent:
questions.why: 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series give 5 Ω. Then 5 Ω in parallel with 5 Ω gives 2.5 Ω.

questions.q: Heat produced when 0.5 A flows through 200 Ω for 5 minutes:
In an F2 of 100 plants from a TT × tt cross, 75 are tall. The expected number with genotype Tt is
questions.why: The F2 genotypes are in the ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so half of 100 plants, 50, are Tt.

questions.q: A concave mirror of R = 40 cm. Where must an object be placed to get a virtual image twice its size?
questions.why: f = R/2 = −20 cm. For a virtual image twice the size, m = +2 so v = −2u. Then 1/v + 1/u = 1/(2u) = −1/20, which gives u = −10 cm.

questions.q: An element X forms an oxide X₂O₃ that reacts with both HCl and NaOH. X is likely
questions.why: An oxide that reacts with both HCl and NaOH is amphoteric. Al₂O₃ is amphoteric, so X is aluminium.

questions.q: Why does a ray of light passing through the optical centre of a thin lens go undeviated?
options: Near the centre the two lens surfaces are nearly parallel, like a thin slab
The lens has no refractive index there
questions.why: Near the optical centre the two faces of the lens are nearly parallel, like a thin slab of glass. So the ray goes through almost undeviated.

questions.q: A household has a 5 A circuit. Which set can safely run together at 220 V?
options: A 2 kW heater and a 1 kW iron
Three 100 W bulbs and a 75 W fan
questions.why: A 5 A circuit at 220 V can carry up to 1100 W. Three 100 W bulbs and a 75 W fan total 375 W (about 1.7 A), which is safe. The other sets draw more than 1100 W.

questions.q: Ozone depletion would most directly increase
questions.why: The ozone layer absorbs UV radiation. If it is depleted, more UV radiation reaches the Earth.
